items.title: A single-arm phase II trial of Selective Avoidance of nodal VolumEs at minimal Risk (SAVER) in the contralateral N0 neck of patients with p16-positive oropharynx cancer
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Molitoris JK, Witek ME, Ferris MJ, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To report a single arm multi-site phase II study evaluating a reduced contralateral neck elective nodal clinical target volume (enCTV) in p16+ oropharyngeal cancer (p16+OPC). Methods And Materials: Newly diagnosed p16+OPC without contralateral nodal involvement but with clinical or pathological features warranting contralateral elective nodal treatment were eligible. Treatment included proton- or photon-based definitive (chemo)radiation or adjuvant (chemo)radiation following Transoral Robotic Surgery. All patients received SAVER enCTV and the primary endpoint was two-year elective out-of-field contralateral nodal failure. Dosimetric comparison between SAVER enCTV and consensus enCTV of the first 10 definitive and adjuvant patients was performed. Overall survival (OS), progression-free-survival (PFS), toxicities, and patient reported outcomes were analyzed. Results: Fifty-two patients were enrolled, of which 36 (69.2%) received definitive (chemo)radiation. Thirty-five (67.3%) had bulky or multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes and 18 (34.6%) had significant smoking history. With median follow-up of 31.0 months (range 13 - 49 months), there were no contralateral nodal failures with an upper limit one-sided 95% confidence interval for contralateral nodal failure of 2.7%. Two-year OS and PFS were 92.2% (95% CI [88.5 - 95.9%]) and 86.2% (95% CI [81.4 - 91.0%]), respectively. Dosimetric comparison demonstrated decreased mean dose (18.3 Gy to 14.1 Gy [p=0.001]) and V30 Gy (20.8% to 11.6% [p=0.003]) to the contralateral parotid with SAVER enCTV. Acute grade 3 toxicity was observed in 13 (25%) patients including 8 (15.4%) who received a gastrostomy tube. There were no grade 4-5 toxicities. Conclusion: Selective avoidance of nodal volumes at minimal risk in the N0 contralateral neck can be safely performed while maintaining excellent regional control in the definitive and adjuvant settings. Dose to contralateral organs at risk and toxicity outcomes were favorable.

items.title: Mitomycin C/5-Fluorouracil Versus Cisplatin/5-Fluorouracil With Hyperfractionated Accelerated Radiotherapy in Locally Advanced Head and Neck Cancer: The ARO 04-01/AHMO Trial
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Budach V, Werner J, Wittlinger M, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Cisplatin-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) is the standard for locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). For cisplatin (CDDP)-ineligible patients, mitomycin C/5-fluorouracil (MMC/5-FU) is the most common alternative, but randomized comparisons are lacking. We compared MMC/5-FU with CDDP/5-FU as concurrent partners of hyperfractionated-accelerated radiotherapy (HART) in unresectable, locally advanced HNSCC. Patients And Methods: In this multicenter phase III trial, 364 patients with stage IVA/IVB (UICC TNM 6th edition) oropharyngeal or hypopharyngeal HNSCC were randomized 1:1 to HART (72 Gy/6 weeks) plus either weekly CDDP 30 mg/m² (n=182) or MMC 10 mg/m² on days 5 and 36 (n=182), both with continuous-infusion 5-FU 600 mg/m²/d on days 1-5. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS); secondary endpoints included freedom from progression (FFP), freedom from distant metastasis (FFDM), local, regional and locoregional control, and toxicity, analyzed by Kaplan-Meier and, post hoc, in a competing-risk framework. Results: After a median follow-up of 87 months, CDDP/5-FU was not superior for OS (10-year OS 23% vs. 18%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.89, 95% CI 0.69-1.15; log-rank p=0.418). In the competing-risk analysis, CDDP/5-FU reduced distant metastasis (5-year cumulative incidence 25.9% vs. 36.1%; subdistribution HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.45-0.96; p=0.031) and progression (45.6% vs. 56.3%; subdistribution HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.55-0.98; p=0.037). Kaplan-Meier estimates were directionally consistent but not significant (10-year FFDM 66% vs. 52%; HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.48-1.02; p=0.060; FFP HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.59-1.05); local, regional and locoregional control (HR 0.80-1.01) and toxicity profiles did not differ. Serum creatinine (p<0.001) and the AE/SAE rate (24.2% vs. 15.4%; p=0.048) were higher with CDDP. Conclusion: ARO 04-01/AHMO did not show superiority of CDDP/5-FU over MMC/5-FU for overall survival. CDDP-based CRT remains the established standard for fit patients; MMC/5-FU is a safe and effective alternative with comparable overall survival and measurably lower nephrotoxicity and cumulative AE/SAE burden for CDDP-contraindicated patients. Trial Registration: DRKS00040575.

items.title: Long-Term Safety and Biochemical Outcomes of 24-Gy Single-Dose Versus Five-Fraction SBRT for Intermediate-Risk Prostate Cancer: Pooled Analysis of Two Independently Randomized Cohorts
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Greco C, Pares O, Pimentel N, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To report mature safety, urinary outcomes, PSA response, and biochemical control after 24-Gy single-dose radiotherapy (SDRT) versus 45 Gy in 5 fractions in two independently randomized PROSINT cohorts of intermediate-risk prostate cancer. Methods And Materials: This pooled analysis included 59 evaluable patients randomized locally (45 Gy/5 fractions, n=30; 24-Gy SDRT, n=29). Treatment-related safety was primary, anchored to grade ≥3 genitourinary (GU) or gastrointestinal (GI) events within 3 months (NCI CTCAE v4.0). Acute and late toxicity were ≤90 and >90 days after treatment, respectively. IPSS was modeled longitudinally using generalized estimating equations; PSA kinetics descriptively and biochemical relapse-free survival (bRFS) by Kaplan-Meier/Cox methods. The analysis was not designed for equivalence or noninferiority; efficacy analyses were exploratory. Results: Median follow-up was 60.2 months. No treatment-related grade ≥3 GU or GI toxicity occurred (0/59; 95% CI, 0%-6.1%). Acute grade 1 GU toxicity was 53.3% with 45 Gy/5 fractions and 75.9% with SDRT (P=.103), and GI toxicity 10.0% and 24.1%, respectively (P=.181); no acute grade 2 events occurred. Late GU grade 1 toxicity was 36.7% with 45 Gy/5 fractions and 62.1% with SDRT (HR, 2.04; 95% CI, 0.96-4.32), whereas grade 2 remained uncommon (3.3% vs 10.3%; HR, 3.19; 95% CI, 0.33-30.71). Late GI toxicity was rare. Overall treatment-related grade ≥2 GU/GI toxicity was 6.8%/3.4%. Despite more frequent clinician-reported low-grade GU events after SDRT, IPSS increased transiently at 1 month and recovered toward baseline by 3 months in both arms; the between-arm difference in 1-month change was 2.7 points (95% CI, -1.80 to 7.16), with no evidence of differing longitudinal patterns (P=.733). PSA suppression was deep and sustained, with median PSA of 0.30 ng/mL after 45 Gy/5 fractions and 0.36 ng/mL after SDRT at 36 months. Eleven biochemical failures occurred (5 after 45 Gy/5 fractions; 6 after SDRT); 60-month bRFS was 85.1% (95% CI, 65.1%-94.2%) versus 80.5% (95% CI, 59.2%-91.5%) (HR, 1.05; 95% CI, 0.31-3.50). Conclusions: Clinically significant treatment-related toxicity was uncommon after both regimens. Low-grade GU events were more frequent after SDRT, while patient-reported urinary symptoms recovered toward baseline in both arms. PSA suppression was deep and sustained, but comparative disease-control estimates remained imprecise. These findings support continued prospective evaluation of 24-Gy SDRT with adequately powered disease-control endpoints.

items.title: Adaptive vs. Non-Adaptive Radiation Dose Escalation in Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Comparison of NRG-RTOG 0617 and 1106 Individual Patient Data
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Miccio JA, Hu C, Kong FM, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: For patients with locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (LA-NSCLC), NRG-RTOG 0617 found that non-adaptive radiation therapy (naRT) dose escalation to 74 Gy worsened overall survival (OS) vs. 60 Gy, while NRG-RTOG 1106 showed PET-adapted RT (aRT) dose escalation was safe. This study compares aRT vs. naRT in LA-NSCLC. Materials And Methods: Patients from RTOG 0617 and 1106 randomized to dose-escalation arms with PET-based staging were included. All received thoracic radiotherapy with concurrent and consolidation carboplatin/paclitaxel without immunotherapy. Outcomes were OS, progression-free survival (PFS), cumulative incidence of local-regional progression (CILRP), and grade 3+ toxicity. Results were adjusted for baseline differences between cohorts. Cox models evaluated survival and logistic regression models evaluated toxicity outcomes. Results: Eighty-four patients received aRT and 184 received naRT (median nominal dose 71 Gy vs. 74 Gy). naRT patients had better performance status (Zubrod 0 58% vs. 44%, p=0.0390 and less Intensity Modulated Radiotherapy (IMRT) (49% vs. 92%, p<0.0001). aRT had lower lung V20 (30% vs. 32%, p=0.0413), mean esophagus dose (27Gy vs. 29Gy, p=0.0017), and trend to lower heart V40 (8% vs. 10%, p=0.0907). Unweighted, aRT had a trend to higher 3-year OS (39% vs. 27%, HR=0.72, 95% CI 0.52-1.01, p=0.0535) and significantly higher CILRP (36% vs. 49%, HR = 0.64, 95% CI 0.43 - 0.95, p=0.0324), with similar PFS (20% vs. 21%, HR=0.95, 95% CI 0.71-1.27, p=0.7214). Weighted analyses showed similar outcomes between cohorts. aRT had lower grade 3+ esophagitis (6% vs. 22%, OR=0.24, 95% CI 0.09-0.63, p=0.0040) and similar hematologic toxicity (36% vs. 33%, OR=1.15, 95% CI 0.66-1.99, p=0.6257). Weighted models confirmed these findings and showed lower grade 3+ pneumonitis (OR=0.114, 95% CI 0.01-0.98, p=0.0478) and cardiotoxicity (OR=0.114, 95% CI 0.01-0.98, p=0.0478) for aRT. Conclusion: aRT had improved CILRP and a trend to improved OS with significantly reduced toxicity and improved dosimetry vs. naRT.

items.title: Study Rationale, Enrollment Characteristics, and Central Review of Clinical Stage: The INTACT Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Singh P, Plets M, Efsthathiou J, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Trimodality therapy (TMT) is an established bladder-preservation approach for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). Accurate clinical staging remains challenging and may affect patient selection, trial design, and interpretation of outcomes. Objective: To describe the design, accrual, and baseline characteristics of the Phase III Randomized Trial of Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy With or Without Atezolizumab in Localized Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer (INTACT) trial and evaluate agreement between site-reported and centrally reviewed clinical stage and the prevalence of high-risk disease features. Design, Setting, And Participants: INTACT is a phase 3 randomized clinical trial that enrolled patients with localized MIBC (stage cT2-T4aN0M0) at 136 US sites between April 2019 and March 2025. For this analysis, 243 patients with available source documentation were randomly selected by the SWOG Statistical Center for central clinical staging review. Interventions: Patients were randomized to physician's choice of concurrent chemotherapy (cisplatin, gemcitabine, or 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin C) and radiotherapy (bladder only or small pelvis; 64-64.8 Gy), with or without atezolizumab (1200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks for 9 cycles). Main Outcomes And Measures: The trial's primary end point is 3-year bladder-intact event-free survival, which is not reported in this analysis. Outcomes for the present analysis included trial accrual, clinical stage distribution, agreement between site-reported stage and the initial independent central reviewer, and prevalence of predefined high-risk features (carcinoma in situ, unilateral hydronephrosis, or tumor >5 cm). Agreement was assessed using Cohen κ and directional disagreement using the McNemar test. Results: Among 485 randomized patients, the median (IQR) age was 73.8 (37.6-93.6) years, 384 (79.2%) were male, 16 (3.3%) were Asian, 33 (6.8%) were Black, and 419 (86.4%) were White. Site investigators classified 398 (82.1%) as stage cT2 and 87 (17.9%) as stage cT3 or T4a. Among 243 patients selected for central review, 201 (82.7%) had site-reported stage cT2 disease and 42 (17.3%) had stage cT3 or T4a disease. Agreement between site-reported stage and the initial independent central reviewer was moderate (κ = 0.48; 95% CI, 0.34-0.62). items.title: Partial-Breast Irradiation Versus Whole-Breast Irradiation for Low-Risk Invasive Breast Carcinoma: 5-Year Results of the Multicenter, Randomized, Phase III IRMA Trial
items.authors: Meduri B, Baldissera A, Iotti C, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: The aim of this study was to investigate whether external-beam accelerated partial-breast irradiation (APBI) provides noninferior local control compared with whole-breast irradiation (WBI). Patients And Methods: We conducted this randomized phase III trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT01803958) in 35 centers. Patients age ≥49 years with invasive breast cancer, resection margins ≥2 mm, tumor diameter ≤3 cm, and pN0-1 were randomly assigned 1:1 to WBI or APBI (38.5 Gy in 10 fractions twice daily). Neither patients nor investigators were masked to treatment allocation. The primary end point was ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence (IBTR), analyzed according to the modified intention-to-treat analysis. We assumed a 5-year IBTR rate of 4% in the WBI group to exclude a 2% increase in the APBI group (90% power; noninferiority margin hazard ratio [HR], 1.5). Results: Between 2007 and 2019, 3,309 patients were randomly assigned (1,652 to APBI, 1,657 to WBI); 84 were excluded from the analysis. The median follow-up was 97.5 months. The 5-year cumulative IBTR incidence was 1.0% (95% CI, 0.6 to 1.6) for APBI and 0.8% (95% CI, 0.5 to 1.4) for WBI. The HR for APBI versus WBI was 1.18 (90% CI, 0.63 to 2.20) with the upper confidence limit crossing the prespecified noninferiority margin. Conclusion: At 5 years, the cumulative incidence of IBTR is exceptionally low (≤1%) in both arms. Although formal statistical noninferiority was not demonstrated because the upper confidence limit crossed the margin, the absolute difference was <0.2%. External-beam APBI therefore is a reasonable clinical alternative to WBI for low-risk patients.

items.title: Natural ligand-based CAR T-cell therapy targeting BCMA and TACI for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (TriPRIL): a non-randomised, phase 1, first-in-human trial
items.authors: Puliafito BR, Graham CE, Raje NS, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Functional loss of B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) is a recognised mechanism of relapse after BCMA-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Targeting multiple tumour antigens simultaneously with a single CAR has the potential to mitigate antigen escape and prolong disease responses. Transmembrane activator and CAML interactor (TACI) and BCMA are both highly expressed on most myeloma cells and bind to the same natural ligand-a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL). We designed TriPRIL, a CAR that uses an engineered trimeric form of APRIL, to target both BCMA and TACI. We aimed to establish the safety, tolerability, preliminary efficacy, and recommended phase 2 dose of autologous TriPRIL CAR T cells. Methods: In this first-in-human, open-label, dose-escalation and dose-expansion, phase 1 study, we evaluated TriPRIL in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma at Massachusetts General Hospital (Boston, MA, USA). Eligible patients had received at least three previous lines of therapy or had triple-class refractory disease. Previous CAR T-cell therapy and bispecific antibody therapy exposure were permitted. Patients received 3 days of lymphodepletion with intravenous cyclophosphamide (300 mg/m2) and intravenous fludarabine (30 mg/m2) daily on days -5, -4, and -3 before intravenous TriPRIL infusion on day 0. In the dose escalation phase, patients received 1·0 × 108 or 3·0 × 108 TriPRIL CAR T cells to establish the recommended phase 2 dose, which was further evaluated in the dose expansion phase. The primary endpoint was the incidence of study-related adverse events (graded according to Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5) and dose-limiting toxicities in all patients who received an infusion of TriPRIL CAR T cells, until study completion at 24 months or progressive disease. The data cutoff date was March 24, 2026, when all infused patients had completed at least one assessment of disease response. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05020444), has fully accrued, and is ongoing. Findings: Between Sept 17, 2021, and Jan 27, 2026, 16 patients were enrolled and underwent leukapheresis, with 15 patients subsequently receiving a TriPRIL cell infusion. items.title: Prostate and pelvic nodal stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) versus prostate-only SBRT for high-risk, localised prostate cancer (PACE-NODES): early adverse event results from an international, open-label, phase 3, randomised controlled trial
items.authors: Pathmanathan A, Jain S, Cafferty FH, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Radiotherapy to the prostate and pelvic lymph nodes compared with prostate-only radiotherapy has shown benefits for high-risk prostate cancer in some studies, but evidence remains unclear. In low-risk or intermediate-risk disease, prostate-only stereotactic body radiotherapy (P-SBRT) is safe and effective. PACE-NODES aims to demonstrate safety and efficacy of prostate and pelvic nodal SBRT (PPN-SBRT) for high-risk disease. Methods: PACE-NODES is a phase 3, open-label, randomised trial conducted at 47 hospitals in the UK, Ireland, and New Zealand. The trial recruited men aged 18 years or older, with a WHO performance status of 0-2, and with high-risk (Gleason score 8-10, stage T3a-T4, or prostate-specific antigen >20 ng/mL), localised prostate adenocarcinoma, planned for at least 12 months of hormone therapy. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1), using minimisation with a random element, to P-SBRT (36·25 Gy prostate) or PPN-SBRT (36·25 Gy prostate, 25 Gy pelvic nodes) in five fractions, on alternate days. Neither participants nor researchers were masked to treatment allocation. The primary endpoint is time to biochemical or clinical failure (not yet mature). This preplanned safety analysis is on secondary endpoints, with a focus on Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade 2 or worse gastrointestinal and genitourinary adverse events within 12 weeks of treatment, analysed by treatment received. Patient-reported outcomes include Expanded Prostate Index Composite Short Form (EPIC-26), International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), and EQ-5D-5L. This study is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05613023) and is ongoing. Findings: Between Sept 9, 2022, and July 31, 2025, 1166 participants were recruited and randomly assigned (583 per group). The median age was 72·7 years (IQR 67·7-76·5). 18 patients did not receive radiotherapy; a further 60 (17 assigned to P-SBRT, 43 assigned to PPN-SBRT) did not receive allocated radiotherapy, mostly where planning constraints were not met. This analysis includes 555 patients receiving P-SBRT and 511 patients receiving PPN-SBRT who had completed acute follow-up. Median follow-up was 13·8 months (IQR 7·8-21·0). 118 (21·3%) of 555 patients receiving P-SBRT and 143 (28·0%) of 511 receiving PPN-SBRT had grade 2 or worse gastrointestinal events within 12 weeks (difference 6·7 percentage points [95% CI 1·6-11·9]; p=0·011; odds ratio [OR] 1·44 [95% CI 1·09-1·91]).…

items.title: The cautionary tale of applying the ESMO-MCBS instrument to assess radiation dose escalation for prostate cancer
items.authors: Riaz A, Sapir E, Yu JB, et al.
items.abstract: Background: European Society for Medical Oncology Magnitude of Clinical Benefit Scale (ESMO-MCBS) is widely used to assess clinical benefit of cancer therapies; however, its reliance on overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS) may not adequately capture meaningful benefits in localized prostate cancer, a disease with prolonged natural history. We applied ESMO-MCBS v2.0 to standard-fractionation radiation dose-escalation and examined whether alternative endpoints could better capture clinical benefit. Methods: Randomized clinical trials evaluating standard-fractionation radiation dose-escalation in prostate cancer were identified through PubMed, Google Scholar, and relevant clinical guidelines. Eligible studies were independently assessed by three reviewers using ESMO-MCBS v2.0 based on OS and DFS. Results: Of 51 studies screened, 8 were eligible for grading. One study demonstrated 11% survival gain on mature data and scored grade A. One demonstrated clinically meaningful DFS benefit and would have scored grade B had DFS been primary endpoint. The remaining six studies were not scoreable, primarily because they did not demonstrate improvement in OS or DFS. Several studies demonstrated benefits in distant metastasis (DM), initiation of salvage therapy, or biochemical recurrence (BCR). Conclusions: ESMO-MCBS v2.0 identified clinically meaningful benefit in only one study of radiation dose-escalation in localized prostate cancer. Despite evidence supporting DM as surrogate for OS, it is not scorable in the current framework. Prolonged natural history of prostate cancer and availability of effective salvage therapies may delay DFS and death, further limiting scale's applicability. Additional endpoints warrant evaluation as potential surrogates or indicators of patient-benefit.

items.title: French AFU Cancer Committee Guidelines - Update 2026-2028: Prostate Cancer - Treatment of relapse and metastatic disease
items.authors: Ploussard G, Dariane C, Mathieu R, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: The Cancer Committee of the French Association of Urology (CCAFU) proposes an update of the recommendations for the management of recurrent and/or metastatic prostate cancer (PCa). Methods: A systematic review of the literature from 2024 to 2026 was conducted by the CCAFU to examine the elements of therapeutic management of recurrent prostate cancer after local or metastatic treatment, evaluating the references and their level of evidence. Results: Molecular imaging is the standard assessment for recurrence after local treatment. Its use should not delay early salvage therapy. Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is the cornerstone of treatment for metastatic prostate cancer (PCa). Intensification of ADT, combined with at least one androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI), is now a standard of care for metastatic PCa. Other agents may be added depending on tumor characteristics and patient eligibility. Radiation therapy of the primary tumor is standard for patients with low tumor volume or fewer than 5 metastases on conventional imaging. For patients with castration-resistant PCa (CRPC), PARP inhibitors and PSMA-guided internal radiotherapy are newer treatment options. The combination and sequencing of treatments depend on numerous factors (patient and disease characteristics, prior lines of therapy, genomic status, and molecular imaging). Conclusion: This update of the French recommendations should contribute to improving the management of patients with recurrent or metastatic prostate cancer.

items.title: Which Patients with Advanced Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma Benefit Most from First-line Checkpoint Inhibitor Combination Regimens: A Meta-analysis of Individual Patient Data and Aggregate Data from Randomised Trials
items.authors: Richters A, Westgeest HM, Özdemir BC, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Objective: To quantify heterogeneity in the treatment effects of first-line immuno-oncology (IO)-based combination regimens among patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC) according to prognosis and potential effect modifiers and to assess which patients benefit most. Methods: Meta-analysis (preregistered in PROSPERO: CRD42023483638) including randomised trials underpinning first-line IO-based regimens recommended in the European Society for Medical Oncology 2024 guidelines using sunitinib as control, with mature overall survival (OS) data available as of November 2023. Individual patient data (IPD) were obtained for two trials and aggregate data for two others. Prognostic stratification was performed by the International Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Database Consortium (IMDC) model and, for IPD trials, by the Clinical Prognostic Index in the Checkpoint Inhibitor era (CPI2) model. Effect modification by sex and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression was assessed. OS benefit was summarised as a hazard ratio (HR) and, in IPD, as the difference in restricted mean survival time (dRMST), and was pooled across trials using fixed-effects inverse-variance-weighted models. Key Findings And Limitations: CheckMate-214, CheckMate-9ER, KEYNOTE-426 and CLEAR were included, totalling 3320 patients (IPD for CheckMate-214 and CheckMate-9ER; n = 1747). Among IPD studies, 42%, 32%, and 26% of patients had CPI2 favourable, intermediate, and poor prognosis, respectively. The respective pooled subgroup dRMSTs were 1.21 (95% CI = -0.82 to 3.25), 3.15 (0.50 to 5.81), and 7.36 (4.56 to 10.17) mo. Using all four studies, the pooled HRs for IMDC favourable, intermediate, and poor subgroups were 0.98 (0.81 to 1.19), 0.78 (0.68 to 0.89), and 0.51 (0.40 to 0.65), respectively. PD-L1 expression at 5% significantly modified the treatment effect. Conclusions And Clinical Implications: IO-based regimens showed highly divergent OS efficacy across prognostic subgroups, with no significant benefit among patients with a favourable prognosis and the strongest benefit in patients with a poor prognosis.

items.title: Single- Versus Two-Fraction HDR Brachytherapy Boost for Prostate Cancer: Long-Term Oncologic and Toxicity Outcomes
items.authors: Goñi A, Sevilla M, Larruskain M, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: High-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy boost with external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) is an established dose-escalation strategy for high-risk prostate cancer, but the optimal number of HDR fractions is unclear. We compared oncological outcomes and toxicity between single- and two-fraction HDR boost. Materials And Methods: Retrospective cohort of 378 patients with localized prostate cancer treated as high risk by institutional criteria (D'Amico-based; regrouped by NCCN) in 2004-2016 with EBRT (46 Gy) and a CT-guided HDR boost. Before November 2009, patients received EBRT followed by two HDR fractions of 9-10 Gy 8 hours apart (n=205); from November 2009, a single 15 Gy fraction preceded EBRT (n=173). Biochemical recurrence-free (BRFS), metastasis-free, cancer-specific (CSFS), and grade ≥3 genitourinary (GUTFS) and gastrointestinal toxicity-free survival were estimated with Kaplan-Meier and compared with the log-rank test; Cox models were fitted. Results: Median follow-up was 130.1 months (IQR 94-158). Single-fraction patients more often had cT3 disease (72.3% vs. 43.4%) and NCCN high or very high risk (84.4% vs. 67.8%). At 10 years, BRFS, MFS, and CSFS were 81.4%, 91.5%, and 95.4%, without significant differences between one and two fractions (BRFS 79.6% vs. 82.6%, p=0.784; CSFS 95.3% vs. 95.4%, p=0.992). Crude grade ≥3 GU toxicity was higher with two fractions (22.9% vs. 10.4%, p=0.002); 10-year GUTFS was 82.2% vs. 89.7% (p=0.076). PSA and Gleason score >7 independently predicted CSFS and BRFS. Conclusion: In this non-randomized comparison of consecutive protocols, one and two HDR boost fractions showed no significant difference in long-term oncological control. The confidence intervals were wide, and equivalence was not tested. Two fractions had more grade ≥3 GU toxicity, which cannot be separated from treatment era, EBRT sequence, and follow-up. A single 15 Gy fraction appears adequate as a boost combined with EBRT. It does not apply to HDR monotherapy. Prospective confirmation is needed.

items.title: AI-Assisted Contour Quality Assurance in a Multi-Center Genitourinary Clinical Trial: Feasibility Results from NRG-GU010
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Geng H, Karrison T, Desai NB, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Expert contour quality assurance (QA) in multi-center radiation therapy trials is labor-intensive and scales poorly. We evaluated whether an FDA-cleared AI auto-segmentation tool can serve as a high-sensitivity screening aid for contour QA in the genitourinary (GU) trial NRG-GU010. Methods And Materials: Data from 579 patients submitted to NRG-GU010 (NCT05050084) were studied in two cohorts: the first 52 consecutive submissions (one excluded for an unavailable planning CT; 51 analyzed) for a consensus-based agreement analysis, and the subsequent 527 for large-cohort workflow validation. AI-generated contours were compared with submitted contours using four geometric indices (Dice similarity, Hausdorff distance, mean distance to agreement, percent volume change) against thresholds from prior per-protocol cases, producing target-volume (TV) and organ-at-risk (OAR) scores of 1 (per-protocol), 2 (acceptable variation), or 3 (unacceptable deviation). The 51-case cohort used multi-expert adjudicated consensus as reference; the 527-case cohort used each case's single reviewing principal investigator (PI) under a triage framework (AI-positive = score 2 or 3; PI-positive = score 3). Agreement was assessed with quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa; sensitivity and specificity are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: In the consensus cohort, AI identified all four unacceptable (score-3) OAR deviations (sensitivity 1.00; 95% CI, 0.40-1.00); no consensus score-3 TV cases were present. Quadratic-weighted kappa was 0.71 (0.40-0.90) for OAR and 0.53 (0.31-0.74) for TV. In the 527-case validation cohort, AI triage sensitivity was 100% for both TV (5/5) and OAR (4/4) score-3 deviations, with case-level specificity of 69% (TV) and 25% (OAR) and 100% negative predictive value for both. Conclusions: AI-assisted contour comparison served as a high-sensitivity triage tool, flagging all clinically unacceptable deviations while clearing AI-negative cases, supporting its use as a screening aid-not a replacement-for expert contour QA in GU clinical trials. Lower specificity (particularly for OARs) and few score-3 events warrant further disease-site-specific validation.

items.title: French AFU Cancer Committee Guidelines - Update 2026-2028: Muscle-invasive bladder tumors (MIBC)
items.authors: Roumiguié M, Marcq G, Bajeot AS, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: To update the CCAFU guidelines for the management of muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). Methods: A systematic review (Medline) of the literature from 2024 to 2026 was performed, considering the diagnostic work-up, treatment options, and NMIBC and MIBC follow-up, with references graded according to their level of evidence. Results: The diagnosis of muscle-invasive bladder cancer relies on transurethral resection of the bladder. The staging work-up includes CT urography combined with chest CT. Multiparametric bladder MRI may be proposed to refine locoregional assessment without delaying management. For nonmetastatic disease, radical cystectomy with standard pelvic lymph node dissection remains the reference treatment. In cisplatin-eligible patients, a perioperative strategy based on cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy should be discussed, with consideration of integrating immunotherapy and perioperative systemic treatment according to available indications. The combination of enfortumab vedotin and pembrolizumab (EVP) is also recommended. In cisplatin-ineligible patients, EVP represents a major therapeutic option when available. A bladder-sparing strategy using trimodal therapy-combining maximal transurethral resection, external beam radiotherapy, and concomitant radiosensitizing chemotherapy-should be discussed and offered to selected, well-informed patients who are compliant with rigorous follow-up. Urinary diversion by enterocystoplasty may be offered to both men and women in the absence of oncologic, functional, or general contraindications; otherwise, ileal conduit urinary diversion remains the reference diversion. Enrollment in an enhanced recovery program after surgery is recommended for all surgical patients. For metastatic disease, the EVP combination is the recommended first-line treatment. After disease progression, subsequent therapeutic options should be tailored according to previously received treatments, patient profiles, potential molecular alterations, and access to clinical trials. Conclusion: This update of the CCAFU guidelines aims to harmonize and optimize the management of patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, incorporating recent developments in diagnostic work-up, perioperative treatments, bladder-preservation strategies, and the management of metastatic disease.

items.title: French AFU Cancer Committee Guidelines - Update 2026-2028: Kidney cancer
items.authors: Bigot P, Khene ZE, Margue G, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: To update recommendations for the management of kidney cancer. Methods: A systematic review of the literature published between 2014 and 2026 was performed to identify relevant evidence on diagnosis, classification, treatment, and follow-up. Recommendations were graded as strong or weak. Results: Contrast-enhanced thoraco-abdominal CT remains the reference for diagnosis and staging, while PET/CT is not routinely indicated. Percutaneous biopsy is recommended when it may influence therapeutic decision-making and reduce unnecessary surgery for benign tumors. Tumors are classified according to the 2017 pTNM classification (revised in 2025), the 2022 WHO classification, and ISUP grade; metastatic disease is stratified by IMDC risk group. For T1 tumors, minimally invasive robot-assisted partial nephrectomy is the reference surgical treatment. Active surveillance should be offered for masses≤2cm regardless of age and may be considered for selected tumors up to 4cm. Ablative therapies and stereotactic radiotherapy are alternatives for patients unsuitable for surgery. Radical nephrectomy remains the standard for locally advanced disease, and adjuvant pembrolizumab is recommended for patients at high risk of recurrence. Immediate cytoreductive nephrectomy is not recommended in poor-risk metastatic disease. First-line treatment of metastatic clear cell RCC relies on immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations according to IMDC risk. Clinical trial enrollment should be prioritized after progression on adjuvant pembrolizumab and in later treatment lines. Patients with non-clear cell RCC should undergo expert multidisciplinary review, with priority given to clinical trials. Appropriate use of healthcare resources and environmental sustainability are integrated throughout the recommendations. Conclusions: These updated recommendations incorporate recent advances in diagnosis, surgery, systemic therapy, and disease monitoring, providing a contemporary evidence-based framework for the management of kidney cancer across disease stages.

items.title: Carfilzomib-based strategies in transplant-eligible multiple myeloma: long-term follow-up of the phase 2 FORTE trial
items.authors: Bertuglia G, D'Agostino M, Rota-Scalabrini D, et al.
items.abstract: In the phase 2 FORTE trial, transplant-eligible newly diagnosed multiple myeloma patients aged ≤65 years were randomized to (R1) carfilzomib-lenalidomide-dexamethasone followed by autologous stem cell transplantation (KRd-ASCT), twelve cycles of KRd (KRd12), or carfilzomib-cyclophosphamide-dexamethasone followed by ASCT (KCd-ASCT). Eligible patients were then randomized (R2) to maintenance with carfilzomib for 2 years plus lenalidomide until progression (KR) or lenalidomide alone until progression (R). With extended follow-up (median 99 months from R1 and 85 months from R2), KRd-ASCT significantly increased progression-free survival (PFS, median 98 months) versus KRd12 (median 70 months; HR 0.71, p=0.027) and KCd-ASCT (median 67 months; HR 0.66, p=0.006). A significant benefit in PFS2 was also observed versus both KRd12 (HR 0.65, p=0.02) and KCd-ASCT (HR 0.68, p=0.04) and in terms of overall survival (OS) versus KCd-ASCT (8-year OS: 76% vs 68%; HR 0.65, p=0.04). KR maintenance significantly improved PFS versus R (HR 0.67, p=0.02), with a time-dependent effect persisting up to two years after carfilzomib discontinuation; no differences in PFS2/OS were observed. KR significantly increased rate of measurable residual disease (MRD) conversion (sHR 0.47, p=0.03) during active treatment, and reduced MRD resurgence (sHR 0.53, p=0.001) versus R. Median duration of MRD negativity was 50.5 months in KR vs. 38 months in R arm. MRD-negative patients had significantly prolonged PFS with KR (HR 0.60, p=0.031); MRD-positive patients benefited from KR mainly during carfilzomib therapy (HR 0.46, p=0.05). The cumulative incidence of second primary malignancies was 6%. In conclusion, long-term follow-up confirms the high effectiveness of KRd-ASCT and KR maintenance. NCT02203643.

items.title: A Phase I/II Trial of the Metalloporphyrin Radioprotectant BMX-001 in Patients with Newly Diagnosed Head and Neck Cancer Receiving Concurrent Radiation Therapy and Cisplatin
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Salans M, Yom SS, Dufault SM, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose/Objectives: MnTnBuOE-2-PyP5+ (BMX-001) is a manganese metalloporphyrin superoxide dismutase mimic that inhibits radiation stress-induced pathways and may mitigate treatment-related side effects. We evaluated the safety and efficacy of BMX-001 on severe oral mucositis (OM), xerostomia, dermatitis, quality of life, and patient reported outcomes (PROs) among patients undergoing chemoradiation for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Materials/Methods: This multicenter, phase I/II trial included patients with stage III-IVB HNSCC (AJCC 7th ed) undergoing definitive or postoperative chemoradiation (CRT). Patients received a subcutaneous BMX-001 loading dose followed by twice-weekly maintenance dosing through one week post-CRT at three loading/maintenance dose levels (7/3.5 mg, 14/7 mg, and 28/14 mg), with level 3 expanded for phase II endpoints. OM, xerostomia, and dermatitis were assessed weekly during treatment, within one month, and at six and 12 months post-chemoradiation. PROs and saliva production (stimulated and unstimulated) were measured at baseline, end of CRT, and one, six and 12 months post-CRT. Descriptive statistics summarized adverse events, symptom duration, and PROs. Results: Between 5/2017 and 12/2019, 29 patients were enrolled; 86% had oropharynx primaries (n=25; n=24 HPV+) and 89.7% (n=26) underwent definitive CRT. One patient experienced two serious adverse events possibly related to BMX-001. Grade 3 OM occurred in 41.4% (n=12); acute and chronic grade ≥2 xerostomia occurred in 17.9% (n=5) and 9.1% (n=2), respectively, and 6.9% (n=2) experienced grade 3 dermatitis. At a median follow-up of 24 months, 96.6% were alive without progression. In exploratory longitudinal analyses of the 23 patients treated at the recommended phase II dose, patient-reported symptom and quality-of-life measures generally worsened at the end of CRT and subsequently improved. Several measures were no longer statistically different from baseline by six months, while measures of xerostomia remained elevated. Conclusions: BMX-001 is safe and feasible in patients with advanced HNSCC. In addition, BMX-001 shows promising efficacy for mitigating CRT-associated toxicity and warrants further study in larger, controlled trials.

items.title: Is it tumor burden? A critical analysis of postirradiation lymphopenia in lung cancer patients
items.authors: Kaveckyte V, Bjerrum A, Pøhl M, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: We examined association between treatment‑induced lymphocytopenia and mediastinal lymph node irradiation in locally advanced non‑small cell lung cancer patients and whether disease extent confounds overall survival (OS) analysis. Materials And Methods: Two cohorts were used: A (165 patients) for method development and B (159 patients) for confirmatory evaluation. Auto-segmented mediastinal structure was used as a substitute for lymph node irradiation in the end-of-radiotherapy absolute lymphocyte count (EoRT-ALC) regression models. Comparative EoRT-ALC models with estimated dose to immune cells (EDIC) were developed. In Kaplan-Meier OS analysis the cohorts were stratified by grade 3+ (G3+) lymphopenia before and after accounting for the disease extent via one-to-one propensity score matching. Results: Multivariable models with mean mediastinum dose and EDIC were comparable (adjusted-R2 0.332 vs. 0.337 and 0.253 vs. 0.252 in the A and B cohort, respectively). There was significant difference (p < 0.001 in cohort A, p = 0.03 in cohort B) in OS between the strata with and without G3+ lymphopenia; in cohort A hazard ratio (HR) was 2.29 with 95 % confidence interval (CI) of 1.39-3.77 and in cohort B HR = 1.68 (95 % CI 1.04-2.71). Both strata with G3+ lymphopenia had significantly greater tumor burden and/or nodal stage. After propensity score matching, there was no significant difference (p = 0.30) between the strata; in cohort A HR was 1.42 (95 % CI 0.72-2.80), in cohort B HR was 1.41 (95 % CI 0.73-2.71). Conclusions: The data showed no consensus which structure might need to be spared in future clinical trials. Further, the data suggested that the disease extent might be confounding G3+ lymphopenia association with worse patient OS. Potential benefit of lymphocyte sparing dose planning cannot be concluded.

items.title: Megestrol Acetate for Prevention of Weight Loss During Modern Radiotherapy in Patients With Head and Neck Cancer: A Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial
items.authors: Muangwong P, Samakgarn V, Malasri P, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Weight loss is a common complication during radiotherapy for head and neck cancer and may adversely affect treatment tolerance and outcomes. We evaluated whether megestrol acetate (MA) prevents treatment‐related weight loss. Methods In this multicenter, open‐label randomized controlled trial, 102 patients with non‐nasopharyngeal head and neck squamous cell carcinoma undergoing radiotherapy were assigned to MA plus standard care or standard care alone. Standard care consisted of nutritional counseling, symptom management, and feeding‐tube placement when clinically indicated. The primary endpoint was change in body weight from baseline to 6 weeks post‐radiotherapy. Results At 6 weeks post‐radiotherapy, the MA group showed a mean weight gain of 2.07 kg, whereas the control group lost 1.74 kg (p < 0.01). Weight gain was primarily due to increased fat mass, with no significant difference in muscle mass. Quality of life was similar between groups. Conclusion MA improved weight preservation during radiotherapy and may serve as an adjunct to supportive care in head and neck cancer. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: TCTR20240330005

items.title: Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy vs Surgery for Stage IA Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
items.authors: Linderman GC, Li KQ, Potter AL, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) is a well-established alternative to surgery for nonoperable patients with early-stage non-small cell (NSCLC) lung cancer. However, the role of SBRT in operable patients is unclear as 3 randomized clinical trials comparing SBRT with surgery were closed early because of poor accrual. Existing observational comparisons are limited by confounding because patients who receive SBRT are generally frailer and more comorbid. Objective: To compare cancer-specific mortality between surgery and SBRT using proximal causal inference to adjust for unmeasured confounding due to frailty and comorbidity using proxy variables. Design, Setting, And Participants: This cohort study was a national database analysis of the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER)-Medicare dataset. Three treatment effect estimates were obtained with increasing control of confounding: unadjusted, standard-regression adjusted for measured confounders as in existing studies, and proximally adjusted for unmeasured confounders. Participants were patients with stage IA NSCLC who underwent sublobar resection or SBRT from 2010 to 2019, followed up through December 21, 2021. Data analysis was performed from April 2023 to August 2026. Exposures: Sublobar resection vs SBRT. Negative control exposures were constructed from billing codes. Main Outcome And Measures: Lung cancer-specific mortality. Negative control outcomes were constructed from other-cause mortality. Results are reported as hazard differences (HD) and 95% CI. Results: A total of 4251 patients met inclusion and exclusion criteria; 2581 (60.7%) were female and 1670 (39.3%) were male. Their mean (SD) age was 75.6 (6.3) years. A total of 2558 patients underwent SBRT and 1693 underwent surgery. In the unadjusted and covariate-adjusted analyses, SBRT was associated with higher lung cancer cause-specific mortality, HD of 0.047 person-years (95% CI, 0.038-0.055) and 0.024 person-years (95% CI, 0.014-0.034), respectively. However, there was also compelling evidence of confounding due to a strong estimated association with other-cause mortality. In the proximal analysis, other-cause mortality together with negative control exposures were used to indirectly control for hidden confounders, yielding an HD of 0.012 person-years (95% CI, 0.0013-0.027). Conclusions And Relevance: This study empirically showed that existing observational comparisons of SBRT and surgery are biased because of unmeasured confounding.…

items.title: Induction Immunochemotherapy Followed by Definitive Chemoradiotherapy and Consolidation Immunotherapy for Locally Advanced Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Prospective Phase II Study
items.authors: Lin L, Li H, Song X, et al.
items.abstract: Long-term survival after definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (dCCRT) remains limited in locally advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). We evaluated induction immunochemotherapy followed by dCCRT and consolidation immunotherapy in this setting. This prospective, single-arm Phase II study enrolled 54 adults selected for definitive nonsurgical treatment. The planned regimen comprised two cycles of induction immunochemotherapy with nab-paclitaxel, carboplatin, and a programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitor, followed by dCCRT with 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions and concurrent weekly chemotherapy. The same PD-1 inhibitor was planned as consolidation therapy for up to 1 year. The primary endpoint was the 2-year overall survival (OS) rate. Fifty-three patients (98.1%) completed two induction cycles, all 54 proceeded to dCCRT, and 31 (57.4%) received consolidation immunotherapy. Among all 54 enrolled patients, the 2-year OS and progression-free survival (PFS) rates were 84.6% (95% confidence interval [CI], 75.2%-95.0%) and 61.5% (95% CI, 49.5%-76.4%), respectively, after a median follow-up of 28.1 months. Adverse events occurred predominantly during dCCRT and were mainly hematologic; lymphopenia and esophagitis were among the most frequent toxicities. Exploratory analyses suggested that suboptimal response after induction immunochemotherapy was associated with shorter PFS. The survival outcomes observed with this sequential approach support further evaluation of its comparative clinical benefit in randomized studies. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05621707).

items.title: [Comment] Pelvic nodal SBRT: from feasibility to therapeutic value
items.authors: Darren M C Poon
items.abstract: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT), a type of radiotherapy that delivers highly conformal, high-dose irradiation in a limited number of fractions, is now an established treatment option for localised prostate cancer. The randomised, phase 3 PACE-B and PACE-C studies demonstrated the efficacy of prostate SBRT for patients with low-to-intermediate-risk prostate cancer, and its safety with androgen deprivation therapy in those with unfavourable intermediate-risk or high-risk prostate cancer.1,2 However, the safety of extending prostate-directed SBRT to include elective pelvic nodal irradiation, which requires larger treatment volumes, remains uncertain.

items.title: Benchmarked quality indicators for palliative radiotherapy near end of life: A multinational Delphi project
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Roos D, Govindaraj R, Martinello R, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: The aims of this project were to devise and benchmark internationally applicable quality indicators (QIs) for palliative radiotherapy (RT) "near end of life". To the best of our knowledge, this is the first multinational attempt at consensus on QIs for any palliative RT setting. Methods And Materials: Radiation and clinical oncologists with expertise in palliative RT, and cancer consumer advocates were invited to undertake a Delphi survey. The 30/30 invited panelists comprised 27 clinicians from nine countries and three consumers from XXXX and New Zealand, denoting a replicability in the upper range of "moderate" (defined as 60% to <80%). The panel initially agreed upon a definition of near end of life for patients undergoing palliative radiotherapy ("A state of irreversible functional decline from cancer and a short prognosis often measured in weeks or months"), and a timepoint criterion for benchmarking the subsequent QIs ("Patients dying within 30-days of starting palliative RT"). Nine candidate QIs were curated by the XXXX prior to the voluntary, anonymous survey which utilized an online platform (SurveyMonkey). Responses were appraised by an XXXX steering sub-committee, with 75% agreement defined as the iterative consensus threshold. Results: The response rate for each of four Delphi rounds was 30/30 (100%). Supported QIs for near end of life patients relating to life expectancy documentation (2), waiting time for RT (1) and RT fractionation (2) were each benchmarked at ≥80%, with ≤30% for 30-day mortality. Additionally, the panel benchmarked conventional 30-day mortality (for all palliative RT patients) at ≤20%. Conclusions: Seven QIs were accepted and benchmarked, six for palliative RT near end of life, and one for all palliative RT patients. Real-world testing of the feasibility of these QIs and achievability of the benchmarks is required.

items.title: Estimates of breast cancer screening benefit in older women to inform patient-centered care
items.authors: Schoenborn NL, Blackford AL, Cheung LC, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: When to stop breast cancer screening remains uncertain. The USPSTF recommends screening to age 74. Modeling estimates on screening benefit after age 74 are 5-12 average life-years gained (LYG) per 1000 women, which may be a useful benchmark for considering stopping screening. Existing LYG estimates do not incorporate individualized cancer risk or individualized life expectancy and involve numerous assumptions in simulation models. We aimed to estimate screening benefit in older women that incorporate frailty/comorbidity and breast cancer risk. Methods: Using SEER-Medicare data (1999-2017), we constructed cohorts to estimate screening benefit at age 70 and 75, respectively. We included women continuously enrolled in fee-for-service Medicare for ≥5 years and were breast cancer free before the age of interest. We obtained screening-associated breast cancer mortality risk reductions from a previous emulated trial. We combined these with individualized breast cancer mortality risk and individualized competing mortality risk to calculate average LYG from continuing annual screening over 8 years. Estimates were stratified by race and comorbidity/frailty. Results: Average LYG from screening ranged from 4.7-20.5 life-years per 1000 women in the age 70 cohort (n = 204,288), 3.4-13.6 life-years per 1000 women in the age 75 cohort (n = 193,398). Those with higher comorbidities/frailty had lower average LYG. Those with Hispanic/Asian/other race had the lowest LYG whereas Black women had the highest LYG. Conclusion: Average LYGs from breast cancer screening based on population level data are small in older women, with important variations by health status and race, which should be considered in clinical discussions and screening recommendations.

items.title: Abdominal reirradiation: practice principles from Reirradiation Collaborative Group (ReCOG)
items.authors: Murrell DH, Bergman AM, Corradini S, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Abdominal reirradiation (reRT) is an increasingly common treatment consideration as people live longer due to advances in cancer care. How we deliver courses of reRT still remains individualised and limited prospective data exists to support practice. This Reirradiation Collaborative Group (ReCOG) effort describes principles of practice and insights into clinical approaches for abdominal reRT. Methods And Materials: Six cases demonstrate challenges inherent to abdominal reRT scenarios, including urgent palliation, partial high dose overlap with prior treatment, and when reRT may not be offered. Cases and relevant literature were discussed by an expert panel to offer a structured approach to treatment decision-making and provide guidance for clinical practice. Results: The cases demonstrate scenarios in which abdominal reRT can be an effective treatment and the uncertainties that may arise, requiring individualized treatment. The safety of proposed reRT should be balanced against the probability of side effects from therapy versus sequelae from uncontrolled tumour. This risk-to-benefit ratio can vary considerably depending on the intention of treatment and goals of care which impact decision making. Conclusion: This case-based overview offers practical suggestions from an expert panel on how best to approach challenging cases, while we await a more standardised framework for abdominal reRT.

items.title: Feasibility of DLAS-Driven Reoptimization to Accelerate MR-guided Online Adaptive Radiotherapy for Abdominal Malignancies
items.authors: Conlin R, Chen X, Amjad A, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: MR-guided online adaptive radiation therapy (MRgOART) adjusts for daily anatomical changes. One challenge is prolonged treatment time due to organs-at-risk (OARs) contour editing. Recently, deep learning auto-segmentation (DLAS) models have demonstrated accuracy on MRI images, reducing contour editing demands. In this retrospective study, we investigate the dosimetric impact of DLAS-driven MRgOART, in which daily adaptive plans are created directly using unedited DLAS contours, and the feasibility of a one-step contour and adaptive plan review and approval process. Methods: Six patients treated for abdominal malignancies on a 1.5T MR-Linac were studied. Daily OAR anatomy was segmented by a MR-based DLAS model, with targets rigidly transferred from reference images. The DLAS-driven plan was generated by re-optimizing using unedited DLAS contours. Dose was recalculated using clinical contours for dosimetric comparison with the clinical plan. Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), mean distance-to-agreement (MDA), surface Dice Similarity Coefficient (sDSC), and relative added path length (rAPL) were used to compare geometric accuracy of DLAS to clinical contours. Target coverage, D0.03cc to the gastrointestinal OARs, and V1200cGy to kidneys and liver were used to assess plan quality. Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank tests evaluated dosimetric differences between DLAS-driven and clinically delivered plans. Time savings for contour editing to plan approval were estimated. Results: DLAS and clinical contours demonstrated good agreement, with most average DSC scores exceeding 0.8 and average MDA under 3mm for OARs. No significant differences were found in target coverage, D0.03cc, or V1200cGy between the clinically delivered and DLAS-driven plans. Estimated treatment time savings ranged from 8 to 24 minutes. Conclusions: Accurate MR-based DLAS models may enable DLAS-driven adaptive planning, eliminating contour edits prior to reoptimization. DLAS-driven plans were comparable to clinically delivered plans for the six patients studied. DLAS-driven adaptive planning is a promising approach to reduce physician burden and treatment times in MRgOART.

items.title: Computed Tomography Screening and Small Cell Lung Cancer Stage Shift and Survival
items.authors: Potter AL, Kothagundla S, Ananthanarayanan A, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Lung cancer screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) has been shown to identify lung cancers at earlier stages and to significantly reduce lung cancer mortality in prior randomized clinical trials. However, the benefit of LDCT screening for small cell lung cancer (SCLC), an aggressive subtype of lung cancer, is unclear. Objective: To investigate the characteristics and outcomes of SCLC diagnosed after a lung cancer screening examination using a large database of Medicare beneficiaries. Design, Setting, And Participants: In this retrospective cohort study, Medicare data linked to the Surveillance Epidemiology End Results Program's cancer registry data were analyzed. Patients in the US aged 65 to 78 years who were diagnosed with SCLC from 2015 to 2021 were identified for analysis, with follow-up data through 2022. Patients who underwent 1 or more LDCT lung cancer screening examinations during the 12 months preceding their SCLC diagnosis were included in the screened group. All other patients were included in the unscreened group. Data were analyzed from January to August 2026. Exposure: One or more LDCT lung cancer screenings during the 12 months preceding SCLC diagnosis. Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcomes were stage at SCLC diagnosis and overall survival after SCLC diagnosis in the screened and unscreened groups. Results: A total of 17 099 patients (median [IQR] age, 72.0 [69.0-75.0] years; 8999 [52.6%] female) met study inclusion criteria, of which 949 (5.5%) were included in the screened group and 16 150 (94.5%) were included in the unscreened group. When compared with patients in the unscreened group, patients in the screened group were significantly less likely to be diagnosed with distant disease (419 of 949 [44.2%] vs 11 376 of 16 150 [70.4%]; P < .001). Patients in the screened group also had significantly better overall survival when compared with patients in the unscreened group (3-year overall survival, 28.0% [95% CI, 24.9%-31.2%] vs 10.8% [95% CI, 10.3%-11.3%]; P < .001). Both findings were consistent in propensity score-matched analysis. Conclusions And Relevance: Results of this cohort study of Medicare beneficiaries diagnosed with SCLC suggest that receipt of lung cancer screening was associated with a shift toward earlier-stage SCLC at diagnosis and improved overall survival.

items.title: Standardization and pitfalls of iENE in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: Optimizing diagnostic accuracy, prognostic staging and treatment selection
items.authors: De Felice F, Goanta L, Marchi F, et al.
items.abstract: Extranodal extension (ENE) represents the cornerstone of adverse nodal staging in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). While pathological ENE (pENE) is the historical benchmark, the clinical push toward non-surgical primary organ preservation and surgical de-escalation has forced reliance on imaging-derived ENE (iENE). However, applying iENE to clinical decision-making introduces significant methodological and clinical dilemmas. Inspired by recent insights from radiotherapy de-intensification trials in oncology, where "less is not simple" and non-superiority is frequently misconstrued as non-inferiority, this critical review evaluates the evolution of iENE. We critically analyze the transition from unstandardized radiological reporting - "the pre-consensus era" - to international consensus frameworks - "the standardized reporting era" -, dissect the trade-offs between sensitivity, specificity, and disease prevalence and evaluate the incorporation of iENE into the 9th Edition UICC/AJCC TNM staging system. Ultimately, we distinguish the utility of iENE across three distinct clinical objectives: identifying pathological ENE, predicting oncological outcomes for staging and selecting patients for surgery versus chemoradiotherapy.

items.title: Local Treatment for Perineal and Perianal Rhabdomyosarcoma: Clinical Practice Guidelines and Consensus Statement From the Children's Oncology Group, European Pediatric Soft Tissue Sarcoma Study Group, the Cooperative Weichteilsarkom Studiengruppe, and the International Soft Tissue Sarcoma Consortium
items.authors: Seitz G, Martynov I, Fuchs J, et al.
items.abstract: Local control of rhabdomyosarcoma in the perianal and perineal region (PRMS) is challenging due to the unfavorable tumor location, the often advanced stage of disease, the prevalence of alveolar histology with PAX3/FOXO1 fusion, and frequent regional lymph node (LN) involvement at presentation. Distant metastases are present at diagnosis in up to 49% of patients. Given the high risk of recurrence, the prognosis of patients with PRMS treated with multimodal treatment is poor, with a reported 5-year overall survival (OS) rate of 39%-52%. Due to the rarity of PRMS along with variations in treatment protocols over time and across different cooperative groups, we have developed consensus local treatment guidelines. This guideline is based on a comprehensive literature review and expert opinion and is endorsed by the International Soft-Tissue Sarcoma Consortium (INSTRuCT). It integrates insights from three leading pediatric oncology cooperative groups: the Cooperative Weichteilsarkom Studiengruppe (CWS; since December 2024 part of European pediatric Soft-tissue sarcoma Study Group [EpSSG]), Children's Oncology Group (COG), and EpSSG. This document addresses surgical therapy options, including biopsy, nodal staging, and various resection modalities, as well as options for radiotherapy, such as intensity-modulated radiation therapy, proton beam therapy, and brachytherapy.

items.title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgery versus chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced cervical cancer
items.authors: Athanasiou A, Bowden SJ, Ellis LB, et al.
items.abstract: Rationale: Chemoradiotherapy (CRT) is the primary treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC). However, CRT is associated with high toxicity, and access to radiotherapy infrastructure remains limited or unavailable in some settings globally. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) followed by radical surgery has therefore been proposed as an alternative to CRT, but the evidence regarding its efficacy and toxicity compared to CRT remains unclear. Objectives: To compare NACT followed by radical surgery versus CRT for LACC. Search Methods: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov up to 20 May 2026, with no date or language restrictions. We also searched the reference lists of included studies and contacted experts in the field. Eligibility Criteria: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) in women with LACC (FIGO 2018 stage IB3/IIA2/IIB/IIIA-C/IVA) comparing NACT followed by radical surgery to CRT. We excluded non-randomised studies. Outcomes: Our critical outcomes were overall survival, disease-free survival, and progression-free survival. Important outcomes included recurrence, acute and late toxicity, and quality of life. Risk Of Bias: We assessed risk of bias in the included studies using Cochrane's RoB 1 tool. Synthesis Methods: We performed a random-effects meta-analysis using the inverse-variance method. We assessed the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. Included Studies: Three RCTs (from four reports), with a total of 1326 women, reported on the outcomes of interest and were included in the meta-analysis. Synthesis Of Results: NACT + radical surgery may result in little to no difference in five-year overall survival compared to CRT (hazard ratio (HR) 1.11, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.90 to 1.36; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 1259 participants; low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain for five-year disease-free survival (HR 1.28, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.69; 1 study, 635 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and five-year progression-free survival (HR 1.37, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.75; 1 study, 626 participants; very low-certainty evidence). NACT + radical surgery probably increases grade ≥ 3 acute toxicity (risk ratio (RR) 1.82, 95% CI 1.45 to 2.29; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 1224 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain for grade ≥ 3 late toxicity (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.01; 1 study, 591 participants; very low-certainty evidence).…

items.title: Surgical margins in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma: A European Head and Neck Society (EHNS) multidisciplinary modified Delphi consensus
items.authors: Pamuk E, Ferrari M, Kraak JT, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Surgical margin assessment in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) remains poorly standardized by HPV status, subsite, and treatment context. This European Head and Neck Society (EHNS) consensus aimed to harmonize margin assessment and margin-based decisions. Methods: Following systematic review, 25 multidisciplinary panelists evaluated recommendations through two Delphi rounds; consensus was ≥80 % and near-consensus 70-79.9 %. Margindefinitionswerebasedonformalin-fixed,paraffin-embeddedsections,notintraoperativeor postoperativegrossingestimates. Results: Of 48 recommendations, 32 reached consensus, six near-consensus, and 10 were rejected. "Ink on tumor" defined a positive margin irrespective of HPV status (96 %). A 5-mm mucosal margin was retained for HPV-negative OPSCC (84 %), whereas 3 mm reached near-consensus for HPV-positive disease (78.3 %); smaller thresholds were unsupported. A clear margin alone should not determine adjuvant treatment (78.3 %, near-consensus). Re-resection was recommended when the margin site was identifiable and would change adjuvant management. Positive margins warranted radiotherapy in pT1-T2 HPV-positive disease without other adverse features (80 %), whereas chemoradiotherapy was recommended with high-risk features, such as pT3-T4 disease or extranodal extension (95.8 %), and in HPV-negative disease (100 %). For close margins, selective de-escalation could be considered in highly selected HPV-positive disease without high-risk features (82.6 %), whereas HPV-negative disease warranted radiotherapy, with escalation according to additional risks (91.3 %). In fit patients aged ≥70 years with positive margins, radiotherapy alone was favored for HPV-positive disease (87.5 %), while chemoradiotherapy was retained for fit patients with HPV-negative disease (95.7 %). Conclusions: This consensus provides a multidisciplinary framework for harmonized OPSCC margin assessment and risk-adapted postoperative management across HPV status, anatomy, and treatment-related morbidity.

items.title: 2026 Consensus on the Management of Cushing's Disease: A Collaborative Statement from the Korean Endocrine Society and Japan Endocrine Society
items.authors: Park SS, Fukuoka H, Lee J, et al.
items.abstract: The primary treatment goal of Cushing's disease (CD) is sustained normalization of hypercortisolism as well as relief of tumor mass effects, to reduce morbidity and mortality and improve long-term quality of life. Korea and Japan share broadly similar therapeutic principles for CD; however, real-world management differs because of country-specific healthcare systems, regulatory environments, and medication availability. Building on the previously published Korean Endocrine Society (KES)-Japan Endocrine Society (JES) diagnostic consensus, a joint multidisciplinary working group developed an expert consensus focused on the treatment and management of CD. Surgical intervention for pituitary tumors, primarily via a transsphenoidal approach, remains the first-line treatment when feasible. Subsequent treatment should be individualized according to disease and tumor characteristics, severity of hypercortisolism, associated comorbidities, and regional availability of therapeutic options. Medical treatment is recommended for patients with persistent or recurrent disease after surgery, for those who are not candidates for surgery or who decline surgical intervention, and as bridging therapy in severe cases requiring urgent control of hypercortisolemia or when definitive treatment is delayed. Pituitary tumor-directed agents and adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors constitute key pharmacologic options, but the available agents and reimbursement status differ between Korea and Japan. Radiation therapy is considered when surgery is not feasible or when control is not achieved with surgery and/or medical therapy, and bilateral adrenalectomy may be reserved for highly selected refractory cases. This consensus statement provides harmonized, practice-oriented recommendations while acknowledging current evidence gaps and the need for further collaborative research to inform CD management in East Asian populations.

items.title: Long-term preservation of normal brain tissue by minibeam radiation therapy does not require mature T cells
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Bertho A, Roncali L, Lamirault C, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Minibeam radiation therapy (MBRT) preserves normal tissue while maintaining antitumour efficacy, yet the mechanisms underlying this remarkable normal tissue tolerance remain poorly understood. Although adaptive immune responses have been implicated in the antitumour effects of spatially fractionated radiotherapy, their contribution to normal tissue preservation remains unknown. Here, we used a loss-of-function model to determine whether mature T cells are required for the expression of the long-term normal tissue-sparing phenotype associated with MBRT. Methods And Materials: Immunocompetent Fischer 344 rats and athymic nude rats received X-ray MBRT or conventional radiotherapy (CRT) at a mean dose of 30 Gy and were followed for up to six months. Long-term normal tissue response was assessed using complementary behavioural analyses, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and histopathological evaluation of immune infiltration, vascular integrity, glial activation and neuronal survival. Results: Nude rats developed beam-path alopecia and skin lesions earlier than immunocompetent rats and showed a transient reduction in cortical CD31 staining at 7 days post-irradiation, indicating greater acute radiosensitivity without mature T cells. Beyond this early window, the long-term phenotype was comparable between strains: no MRI-detectable lesions, no neuronal loss and no sustained glial activation at 6 months. MBRT induced modest late reductions in exploratory behaviour and recognition memory in both strains, with no significant strain × irradiation interaction. Histologically, MBRT elicited a moderate and transient CD3+ T-cell infiltration that resolved within seven days, whereas CRT induced a stronger and more sustained inflammatory response. Conclusions: Mature T cells modulate the acute tissue reaction to MBRT but are not required for the long-term normal tissue-sparing phenotype. Within the sensitivity of this study, powered for large effects only, mature T cells are unlikely to be a major determinant of long-term MBRT tissue preservation, redirecting attention towards innate immune, vascular and stromal processes.

items.title: EUSICA/INSICA Position Paper on Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Nasal Vestibule: A Distinct Clinical Entity Requiring Dedicated Classification, Treatment Strategies and Outcome Measures
items.authors: de Ridder M, Breimer G, Bossi P, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose Cancer of the nasal vestibule (CNV) differs anatomically and clinically from both sinonasal and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, yet lacks formal recognition as a separate clinical entity and topographical subsite; whether it is also biologically distinct has not yet been investigated. EUSICA/INSICA advocates for formal recognition of CNV and a unified classification, treatment, and translational framework. Method Published literature on CNV, including population‐based cohorts, T‐classification studies, brachytherapy outcomes, and quality‐of‐life data, was reviewed by an international multidisciplinary EUSICA/INSICA expert panel to formulate consensus recommendations. Finding CNV shows favorable outcomes, drains preferentially to facial and submandibular nodes, and is amenable to organ‐preserving radiotherapy, in particular brachytherapy. It is staged using four non‐uniform systems; multicenter validation in 609 patients from 21 centers supported the prognostic utility of the New Rome classification integrated with clinical nodal status. Validated CNV‐specific quality‐of‐life instruments are lacking. Compared with NCCN‐defined high‐risk cutaneous SCC of the nose, CNV differs in topography, pattern of local spread, prognostic landmarks, nodal behavior, and treatment paradigm. Comparative molecular data versus cutaneous and sinonasal SCC are not yet available. Conclusion EUSICA/INSICA calls for formal recognition of CNV as a distinct ICD‐O‐3 subsite, incorporation of the New Rome T classification into UICC/AJCC TNM, standardized organ‐preserving treatment, and dedicated translational research, including comparative molecular studies to determine whether its clinical distinctness has a biological basis.

items.title: Local ablative therapy for oligometastatic non-small cell lung cancer with actionable mutations: A consensus from Hong Kong SBRT Study Group
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Nyaw JS, Kam MT, Lam MY, et al.
items.abstract: Oligometastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is increasingly encountered in clinical practice, owing to advances in imaging techniques and the emergence of new therapeutic options. This manuscript presents the outcomes of a meeting of experts from Hong Kong, convened to review the evidence and provide guidance on the use of local ablative therapies (LATs) for patients with oligometastatic NSCLC harboring actionable mutations. The discussion addressed key topics, including the definitions of oligometastatic and oligoprogressive disease, criteria for selecting patients for radiotherapy and other LAT modalities, optimal radiotherapy dosage, and the sequencing and timing of LATs in conjunction with targeted molecular therapies. Guidance was also developed regarding whether to pause or continue systemic treatments during LAT, and the evidence supporting emerging biomarkers in this context was reviewed. Consensus statements were formulated using a modified Delphi approach, and several case examples were presented to illustrate the application of these recommendations in clinical management. The consensus statements from this meeting could provide an important basis for tailoring treatment for patients with NSCLC who have actionable mutations, as well as pointing out key areas to explore in upcoming research.

items.title: Integrating genetic and lung tissue proteomics data to identify susceptibility proteins for lung cancer
items.authors: Xu S, Shi J, Shu XO, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Proteins directly impact disease development and act as drug targets. We integrated genetic and lung tissue proteomic data to identify lung cancer susceptibility proteins and evaluated them as candidate drug targets. Method: We profiled the proteome and genome in 200 non-neoplastic lung tissue samples and constructed genetic models to predict protein abundance. These models were applied to genome-wide association study (GWAS) data of 55,174 lung cancer cases and 1,294,174 controls to evaluate associations between predicted abundance and lung cancer risk overall and by major histological subtypes. Independent lung tissue proteomic data was used for cross-dataset evaluation, followed by colocalization and summary-data-based Mendelian randomization. Prioritized proteins were cross-referenced against drug databases. Results: We identified 29 lung cancer risk-associated proteins at a false discovery rate < 5%, including 25 for overall lung cancer, two (AQP3 and IL18) specific to adenocarcinoma, and two (HMGN2 and HLA-DMB) specific to squamous cell carcinoma. Genes encoding 15 proteins are located > 2Mb away from known GWAS risk loci. Among the remaining 14 proteins at known risk loci, five (EPHX2, CLDN18, PSMD5, ARHGAP27, and CYP2S1) showed associations independent of proximal lead variant. Of the 29 proteins, eight were predicted and six were significant in independent data. DSP, IL18 and TYMP proteins demonstrated both reproducible and potential causal evidence and are targeted by six drugs that are FDA-approved or in phase III trials. Conclusion: Our study identified novel lung cancer susceptibility proteins and potential therapeutic targets, offering insights into lung cancer biology and informing future translational research.

items.title: Effect of a Multidisciplinary Intervention on Fatigue in Lymphoma Survivors With Persistent Fatigue: A Randomized Controlled Trial (the REFUEL trial)
items.authors: Bøhn SH, Skaali T, Wisløff T, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Persistent fatigue is a prevalent, complex, and distressing late effect among lymphoma survivors. We examined the effect of a multidisciplinary intervention on fatigue among lymphoma survivors with persistent fatigue. Methods: Lymphoma survivors with persistent fatigue (moderate to severe fatigue ≥6 months) were randomly assigned to usual care (n = 75) or a 12-week multidisciplinary intervention (n = 75). The intervention consisted of patient education, physical exercise, a cognitive-behavioral therapy-based program, and nutritional counseling. Total fatigue was assessed by the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (range, 0-33) 3 months after random assignment (T1; primary outcome) and at 6 (T2) and 9 (T3) months after random assignment (secondary outcomes). Other secondary outcomes were functioning and global health status/quality of life (QoL) assessed by European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer QoL Questionnaire-C30. Effects were analyzed with baseline-adjusted linear mixed models for repeated measures. Results: Compared with usual care, the intervention group reported significantly lower total fatigue at T1 (between-group difference [BGD], -3.5 [95% CI, -5.4 to -1.6]; P < .001). Secondary outcome analyses indicated that total fatigue remained lower in the intervention group at T2 (BGD, -2.4 [95% CI, -4.4 to -0.5]), but not at T3 (BGD, -0.9 [95% CI, -3.0 to 1.2]). At T1, secondary outcome analyses indicated positive intervention effects on physical (BGD, 3.8 [95% CI, 0.2 to 7.3]) and role functioning (BGD, 9.2 [95% CI, 0.9 to 17.5]) and global health status/QoL (BGD, 9.5 [95% CI, 3.5 to 15.4]), but not on social (BGD, -0.1 [95% CI, -7.4 to 7.3]), emotional (BGD, 5.6 [95% CI, 0.0 to 11.3]), or cognitive functioning (BGD, 3.5 [95% CI, -3.3 to 10.2]). Conclusion: A multidisciplinary intervention improved fatigue among lymphoma survivors with persistent fatigue. The effect appeared to be maintained 6 months after random assignment but dissipated at 9 months.
