items.title: Patient-reported outcomes results from randomized controlled trials of hematologic malignancies: the impact of trial blinding
items.authors: Efficace F, Cella D, Di Maio M, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are increasingly used in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of hematologic malignancies. However, whether open-label design influences the direction of PRO findings remains uncertain. We assessed whether PRO results from open-label trials are more likely to favor the experimental arm than those from blinded trials. Methods We conducted a systematic review of RCTs in hematologic malignancies published between January 2015 and March 2025 that included PRO endpoints. Trials were classified as open-label or blinded according to patients' awareness of treatment allocation. PRO results were categorized as favoring the experimental arm, favoring the control arm, or showing no difference. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to investigate the association between treatment concealment and PRO results favoring the experimental arm. Other potentially relevant factors, including sample size, publication year, type of experimental treatment, and type of PRO measure, were also included in the analyses. Results We identified 145 RCTs enrolling 59,875 patients. Overall, 104 trials (71.7%) were open-label and 41 (28.3%) were blinded. In univariable analyses stratified by completeness of PRO reporting, treatment concealment was not associated with PRO results favoring the experimental arm. These findings were confirmed in multivariable analyses, with no significant association either among trials with higher completeness of PRO reporting (OR = 0.27, 95% CI = 0.06 to 1.27, P=.097) or among those with lower completeness (OR = 0.31, 95% CI = 0.06 to 1.61, P=.163). Conclusions Our results do not provide evidence that open-label design systematically biases PRO results in favor of investigational treatments in RCTs of hematologic malignancies.

items.title: Field junction technique in MRI-guided ultra-hypofractionated radiotherapy for a long continuous target volume in prostate cancer: First clinical application, dosimetric and early toxicity outcomes
items.authors: Yan L, Qin S, Liang M, et al.
items.abstract: Background: MRI-guided radiotherapy (MRIgRT) on a 1.5 T MR-Linac is constrained by a 22 cm maximum field length, limiting long continuous planning target volumes (PTVs). A dual-isocenter field-junction technique has been previously validated in a phantom study. This work presents its first clinical application in hypofractionated prostate radiotherapy. Materials And Methods: A 79-year-old prostate cancer patient had six contiguous target volumes (PTV, CTV4000, PTVpubis, PGTVpubis, PTVp and PGTVnd), treated over 5 fractions with prescribed doses to the respective target volumes. PTVp was divided into PTVpup and PTVpdn, with a field overlap region between them. Two composite volumes were created: inferior volume (PTV, CTV4000, PTVpubis, PGTVpubis, PTVpdn) and superior volume (PTVpup, PGTVnd), each with its own isocenter. The inferior volume followed the adapt-to-shape (ATS) workflow. During its delivery, the superior volume was first optimized offline on daily MR images using dose feathering approach based on the inferior dose distribution. The optimized plan was then transferred for online adapt-to-position (ATP) adaptation. The inferior and superior volumes were combined offline for dose summation. The ArcCHECK phantom and ArcherQA Monte Carlo method were used for dose verification. Patient-reported outcomes, including FACT-P questionnaires, were collected during the 3-month follow-up. Results: Treatment was delivered over 5 alternate-day fractions. ArcCHECK phantom gamma passing rates, using 3%/2 mm with a 10% threshold, were 96.7%, 97.1%, and 96.0% for the inferior, superior and composite reference plans, respectively. Daily ArcherQA showed consistently high passing rates across five fractions: 97.08%-98.43% for the inferior and 98.12%-98.74% for the superior volumes. CTV4000, PTV, PTVpubis and PGTVpub all met prescribed doses. PGTVnd and PTVp had intermittent underdose relative to initial prescriptions, but all fractions met second prescription limits. Organ at risks (OARs) constraints, especially for rectum and bladder, remained within tolerance across all fractions. Total treatment time decreased from 112 min in the first fraction to 80 min in the fifth fraction. FACT-P score declined from 69.17 at baseline to 55.5 at end-of-RT, partially recovering to 57.5 at 2.5 months. No urological or gastrointestinal toxicity was reported during follow-up. Conclusion: The proposed two-isocenter field junction technique is clinically feasible for MRIgRT of long continuous prostate cancer PTVs.…

items.title: A landscape analysis of access, equity, and reporting trends in digital health randomized controlled trials
items.authors: Harrison TB, Hu D, Chen F, et al.
items.abstract: The merger of technology and healthcare has given rise to a new era of evidence-based medicine. As global regulatory efforts in digital health expand, important questions emerge about who participates in clinical trial evaluations and how findings about digital interventions are documented. To more comprehensively understand equity and access considerations, we conducted a large language model-assisted landscape review to assess technology and study population reporting across 5452 digital health technology-enabled randomized controlled trial outcomes. Between 2010 to January 2024, we observed the compound annual growth rate of digital health trials was over 17%, demonstrating explosive growth as compared to the 9% growth rate across all RCTs with results available on ClinicalTrials.gov during the same timeframe. Digital interventions were consistently described, but reporting of participant characteristics varied. Technology-related eligibility criteria appeared in half of trials, most commonly requiring internet or device access. Age and sex or gender were reported in 98% and 87% of trials, respectively, while other identity characteristics such as race or ethnicity (29%) were less frequently documented. Our findings support a need for amplified global collaboration and consensus building around common data elements toward increasingly equitable and accessible digital health.

items.title: An open agentic AI co-scientist for clinical and biomedical discovery
items.authors: Roberts KF, Abrams ZB, Cappelletti L, et al.
items.abstract: Biomedical research is constrained by the time and domain expertise required to analyze increasingly large and complex datasets. Here we present OpenScientist, an open-source agentic AI co-scientist designed to address this gap by investigating scientist-defined queries and generating verifiable, data-grounded analyses. OpenScientist was evaluated by domain experts across five biomedical case studies, completing analyses in minutes that otherwise would take months of human time and expertise. It accurately quantified Alzheimer's blood biomarker performance, generated a plasma proteomic survival model that predicted survival in a hidden-evaluation cohort, proposed a reproducible mechanism linking tau pathology to altered lysosomal acidification, generated multiple myeloma hypotheses validated in an external cohort with attenuated signal in randomized controls, and demonstrated concordance with an independent human analysis in a blinded, prespecified proteomic comparison. These results support the use of OpenScientist to assist biomedical data analysis in concert with human experts. To support research involving sensitive clinical datasets, OpenScientist can operate in a fully air-gapped environment using open-source models for inference. OpenScientist demonstrates that open, auditable, agentic AI can support real-world clinical research by researching the literature, generating hypotheses, executing analyses, and generating insights from complex datasets.

items.title: Predictors of radiation-induced lymphopenia in NSCLC: blood and bone marrow dose during chemoradiotherapy
items.authors: Nowicka Z, Beekman C, Mohan R, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Radiation-induced lymphopenia (RIL) is a significant complication for patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) undergoing radiotherapy, particularly as immunotherapy becomes increasingly integral to treatment. Understanding the predictors and mechanisms underlying RIL will support and help direct efforts to preserve anti-tumor immunity and optimizing therapeutic outcomes. Methods: This study assessed the relationship between radiation dose to the blood and bone marrow and the development and recovery of lymphopenia in two (training and validation) cohorts, 134 patients in total, with NSCLC treated with either proton (PSPT) or photon-based chemoradiotherapy (CRT) between June 2009 and March 2014. Compartmental blood flow models and automatic organ segmentation were used to quantify radiation doses to circulating blood, large vessels and proliferating bone marrow. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify significant predictors of severe lymphopenia within 2 months from CRT start and its recovery. Results: We found that both the generalized equivalent uniform dose (gEUD) to blood and baseline absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) were significant predictors of grade 4 lymphopenia. The discriminative ability (measured by AUC) for blood dose gEUD peaked around negative alpha values, suggesting that low-dose contributions to the blood pool are most relevant for predicting lymphopenia risk. Despite proton therapy delivering mean blood doses lower by 12.1% (p = 0.006) compared to photon therapy, there were no significant differences in nadir lymphocyte counts between the modalities. Bone marrow dose was only weakly correlated with lymphocyte nadir and showed no association with lymphocyte recovery after treatment. Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that radiation dose to circulating blood is a significant predictor of radiation-induced lymphopenia in NSCLC patients. Despite the observed correlations, these findings suggest that optimizing radiation dose to the blood alone may not be the most effective strategy for reducing lymphopenia.

items.title: Real World Comparison of Asciminib Versus Ponatinib in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia with Propensity Score-Matched Analysis
items.authors: Perusini MA, Kockerols C, Nicolini FE, et al.
items.abstract: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) has an excellent prognosis with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs); however, approximately 40-50% of patients discontinue at least one TKI because of resistance or intolerance. While Ponatinib (PON) is highly effective against resistant disease, Asciminib (ASC) offers robust efficacy with favorable tolerability profile. In the absence of randomized head-to-head trials, we compared outcomes of ASC versus PON using propensity score-matched (PSM) analysis. We conducted a real-world analysis of 762 CML patients previously treated with ≥1 TKI (ASC, n=451; PON, n=311), from an international multicenter cohort. PSM generated 139 balanced pairs after adjusting for age, prior TKI exposure, cardiovascular history, ABL kinase domain mutations, and reason for prior TKI failure. The primary endpoints, evaluated in the matched cohort, were 12-month failure-free survival (FFS) and event-free survival (EFS). ASC was associated with similar molecular response rates and FFS to PON, while EFS was significantly longer with ASC, likely reflecting its more favorable tolerability and lower rate of discontinuation due to intolerance. The difference in EFS was particularly pronounced among patients treated for prior TKI intolerance and in lower-risk subgroups. A sensitivity analysis restricted to patients naïve to both agents (117 matched pairs) confirmed the EFS difference (12-month EFS, 88.6% vs 73.2%; HR 2.48; p=0.002). ASC was associated with similar molecular response and FFS outcomes to PON These findings suggest that ASC was associated with similar real-world molecular response and FFS outcomes to PON, while EFS was longer with ASC, largely driven by differences in treatment discontinuation related to intolerance. ASC may represent an attractive option for patients with prior TKI intolerance, while PON remains an important treatment option for patients with resistant disease.

items.authors: Murray N, Lara Gonzalez LE, Wilcken N, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Patients with large estrogen receptor (ER)-positive, HER2-negative breast cancers have low pathologic complete response (pCR) rates with neoadjuvant chemotherapy. We aimed to determine the rate of tumor downstaging with concurrent neoadjuvant chemo-endocrine therapy (CET) compared with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (CT) in clinical stage 2/3 breast cancer. Methods: This phase II trial randomized women with operable grade 2-3, ER+/HER2- tumors with a primary >20mm 2:1 to neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus concurrent letrozole, or chemotherapy alone. Primary outcome was proportion of tumors down-staged to ≤20mm and ypT0-1ypN0/stage 0-1A. Evaluation of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs), RNA and DNA sequencing were performed to identify correlates of response. Results: ELIMINATE randomized 134 women, with 122 evaluable for the primary outcome. 24% (19/81) with CET and 20% (8/41) with CT (difference 3.9%, 95% CI -11% to 19%) achieved downstaging to ypT0-1ypN0. Overall, 6/122 (5%) had a pCR, all in the CET arm. MRI response was seen in 79% (CET), 66% (CT). Considering grade 3 tumors, 5/22 (23%) in the CET arm and 0/10 in the CT arm achieved pCR. Translational analyses revealed that pCR and RCB 0-I responses were enriched in baseline tumors with higher grade, higher TILs, elevated TMB, and immune activation signatures, independently of treatment arm. Conclusion: CET did not significantly increase downstaging to stage 0-IA. Exploratory analyses suggest a subset of high-grade ER+/HER2- tumors enriched for immune activity, with elevated TILs and high TMB, were associated with favourable response irrespective of treatment assignment. These findings support further exploration of immune-genomic biomarkers in future studies of ER+/HER2- breast cancer.

items.title: Allogeneic umbilical cord-mesenchymal stem/stromal cells for chronic radiation-induced xerostomia: a phase I study with multimodal functional and imaging assessment
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Švajger U, Mitrovič G, Hartman K, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Radiation-induced xerostomia is a clinically significant adverse effect of head and neck radiotherapy with limited treatment options. This prospective, single-arm case series evaluated the safety, feasibility, and exploratory clinical efficacy of ultrasound-guided intraglandular administration of allogeneic umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (UC-MSCs) in patients with chronic radiation-induced xerostomia. Methods And Materials: Ten disease-free survivors of oropharyngeal cancer with CTCAE grade 2-3 xerostomia received ultrasound-guided UC-MSC injections into both parotid and submandibular glands. Each parotid gland received 50 × 10⁶ UC-MSCs and each submandibular gland 25 × 10⁶ UC-MSCs. Safety was the primary outcome. Exploratory assessments were performed at baseline and at 1 and 4 months and included patient-reported outcome measures, unstimulated and stimulated salivary flow rates, salivary biochemical analyses, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasound shear-wave elastography, salivary gland scintigraphy, and, where feasible, core-needle biopsy. Results: No serious adverse events were observed. Procedure-related effects were limited to transient injection-site pain, swelling, and local discomfort. Objective salivary flow rates and most biochemical parameters remained stable throughout follow-up. In contrast, patient-reported outcomes improved, with the greatest changes at 4 months. Xerostomia Questionnaire scores decreased from 63.44 ± 16.81 at baseline to 53.18 ± 21.16 at 4 months (p = 0.0066), and visual analogue scale scores from 64.65 ± 17.30 to 60.29 ± 18.11 (p = 0.0122). Improvements were also observed in xerostomia and sticky saliva domains of the EORTC QLQ-H&N35. MRI showed only subtle changes in T2-weighted signal intensity ratios, while elastography remained unchanged. Scintigraphy demonstrated increased excretion velocity at 4 months (p = 0.0355). Conclusions: In this single-arm case series of 10 patients, ultrasound-guided intraglandular UC-MSC administration was feasible and well tolerated over four months, with no serious adverse events. Improvements in PROMs and scintigraphic excretion velocity were exploratory findings in the absence of a control group and occurred despite largely unchanged salivary flow. Clinical efficacy remains to be established in adequately powered, randomized, placebo-controlled trials.

items.title: Performance of longitudinal cancer screening in Li-Fraumeni syndrome
items.authors: Khincha PP, Ty S, Roy S, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Clinical guidelines recommend multi-modal cancer screening in Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS). However, large-scale, longitudinal data on LFS cancer screening performance are lacking. Methods Generalized estimating equations were used to evaluate the performance of an LFS study cancer screening protocol (NCT01443468) including annual whole-body MRI (WBMRI), brain MRI, breast MRI (females>20 years), mammography (females>40 years), bloodwork, triennial colonoscopy (>25 years), and 4-monthly abdominal ultrasound (ages 3-16 years). Results In 145 participants (62% female), 772 annual screening visits were completed (median 5/participant, range 1-10) with 92.8% adherence.Most cancer/pre-cancer diagnoses (54/72, 75%) were screen-detected; 79.6% were stage/grade 2 or lower. Interval cancers (18/72, 25%) were diagnosed at a median of 8 months (range 3-13) after last screening; 83.3% were ≤ stage/grade 2. The annual asymptomatic cancer detection rate was 4-11%. This protocol had a sensitivity of 71.7%, specificity 89%, positive predictive value (PPV) 15.5%, false positive rate (FP) 11%, negative predictive value (NPV) 99.1%.Overall WBMRI sensitivity was 94%, with specificity 94.8%, FP 27%, and NPV 99.9%. Brain MRI had sensitivity of 85.7%, specificity 98%, FP 2%, NPV 99.9%. Breast MRI had sensitivity of 88.9%, specificity 83.6%, FP 16.3%, NPV 98.9%. Neither TP53 variant class nor participant age significantly affected specificity. A previous cancer diagnosis or false positive in an anatomical region reduced specificity of WBMRI (p < 0.001). Conclusion This longitudinal LFS cancer screening study shows that multi-modal screening performs well, with most cancers being screen-detected at early stages. Further research on alternative screening strategies is needed for interval cancer detection.

items.title: Evaluating a large language model for radiotherapy patient scheduling under realistic clinical and operational constraints: A feasibility study
items.authors: Zhang E, Lai Y, Li W, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Radiation Therapy (RT) scheduling requires coordination of clinical constraints and operational objectives. Large language models (LLMs) may provide a natural‐language interface for generating candidate schedules. Purpose To evaluate the feasibility of using an existing LLM to generate RT patient schedules under clinical and operational constraints through simulation and retrospective clinical comparison. Methods A one‐year, three‐linear‐accelerator (LINAC) simulation included 1400 new patients across 12 treatment categories modeled after clinical practice. Structured prompts supplied ChatGPT with patient data, the current schedule state, clinical rules, and scenario‐specific objectives. Performance was evaluated across scenarios addressing weekly treatment‐time consistency, LINAC continuity, gap‐constrained temporal relaxation, and infeasible request handling. LLM‐generated schedules were benchmarked against heuristic and CP‐SAT schedules under two objective settings. A six‐week retrospective comparison evaluated 2043 appointments against a clinical schedule. Results The LLM‐generated schedules satisfied the predefined feasibility rules in all evaluated scenarios. Across scenarios, 98.6%–98.8% of evaluated fractions remained within the preferred treatment‐time window. Adding a LINAC‐continuity objective reduced the LINAC switch rate from 52.4 ±$\pm$ 2.6% to 9.4 ±$\pm$ 0.6%, and gap‐constrained temporal relaxation reduced daily gap to 47.1 ±$\pm$ 8.5 min and Friday gap to 89.2 ±$\pm$ 18.4 min while maintaining low overtime. In infeasible request tests, the framework identified predefined constraint violations and returned interpretable corrective suggestions. The optimization benchmarks also generated feasible schedules, but their results showed strong objective‐weight trade‐offs. In the retrospective comparison, all computational approaches scheduled the workload without overtime; the LLM strategies reduced mean gap by 50.8%–77.1% and increased time consistency from 86.7% to 99.5%–99.9%. Conclusion Structured LLM‐assisted scheduling was feasible in the simulation and retrospective clinical comparison, producing candidate schedules under predefined constraints. The findings support further investigation of LLMs as flexible, human‐in‐the‐loop decision‐support tools for translating clinical priorities into feasible candidate schedules.

items.title: Factors associated with mood and anxiety disorders in patients with cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.authors: Li M, Zhou X, Deng Z, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Mood and anxiety disorders are common in cancer survivors, and are associated with worse outcomes; however, systematic identification of high‐risk patients remains limited, despite screening and intervention guidelines. A systematic review and meta‐analysis were conducted to identify risk factors for mood and anxiety disorders, including diagnoses and clinically significant symptoms, in adult cancer survivors. Methods PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, PsycINFO, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched for cohort and case‐control studies published from January 2000 to November 2024 that evaluated cancer‐related, sociodemographic, lifestyle, and psychosocial risk factors in adults with breast, lung, colorectal, prostate, stomach, liver, or pancreatic cancer. Random‐effects models with robust variance estimation pooled relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for factors assessed in ≥5 studies. Results Fifty of the 53 eligible studies were included in the meta‐analysis. Consistent risk factors included high tumor stage (vs. low; n = 28; RR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.21–1.97), more physical comorbidities (vs. fewer; n = 36; RR, 1.57; 95% CI, 1.34–1.84), prior psychiatric history (high vs. low burden; n = 13; RR, 4.85; 95% CI, 2.77–8.50), female sex (vs. male; n = 19; RR, 1.52; 95% CI, 1.32–1.75), underweight body mass index (vs. normal; n = 6; RR, 1.93; 95% CI, 1.55–2.44), unmarried status (vs. married; n = 25; RR, 1.35; 95% CI, 1.14–1.58), and current smoking (vs. never; n = 12; RR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.12–1.46). Suggestive associations, although less consistent in sensitivity analyses, were observed for high tumor grade, more extensive surgery, low income, low education, and low social support. Conclusions Several clinical and social factors were associated with increased risk of mood and anxiety outcomes in adult cancer survivors. These findings may support risk‐based psychiatric screening and early intervention in resource‐limited oncology settings.

items.title: Implementation of a 0.55T MR simulator for intracranial stereotactic radiosurgery
items.authors: Kim J, Rusnac R, Dicarlo A, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Low-field MRI has several advantages for radiation therapy simulation. The reduced field strength lowers susceptibility artifacts near metallic implants, decreases intrinsic geometric distortion, and improves safety through lower SAR, reduced projectile risk, and fewer device interactions. MRI is the imaging foundation for SRS target delineation, and initial low-field MRI feasibility for brain radiotherapy planning has been demonstrated in small cohorts. However, SRS clinical implementation has not been reported. We describe the implementation of a 0.55T MR simulator and characterize lesion conspicuity across 102 lesions in 13 patients with multiple brain metastases, drawn from 211 consecutive SRS patients treated to 511 lesions over 12 months. Purpose: To describe the clinical implementation of a 0.55T MR simulator (MAGNETOM Free.Max RT Edition, Siemens Healthineers) as a dedicated radiation therapy simulation system, following a systematic framework of acceptance testing per AAPM TG-284, longitudinal quality assurance, and SRS MRI protocol optimization. Methods: Acceptance testing and commissioning followed AAPM TG-284 recommendations. Testing included the use of vendor-provided homogeneous phantoms, the ACR large phantom, and a commercially available large-field geometric distortion phantom. Longitudinal quality assurance was performed over a 12-month period using the ACR large phantom. Measured parameters included geometric accuracy, percent image uniformity (PIU), percent signal ghosting, low contrast detectability (LCD), and SNR. Contrast to noise ratio (CNR) was calculated for the lesions of a subset of SRS patients having 4 or greater metastatic lesions to evaluate the conspicuity of small SRS lesions in this challenging environment. Results: All acceptance testing met TG-284 recommendations. Central frequency and transmitter gain were stable with changes of less than 0.01% and 0.3%, respectively, over the first month of testing. Geometric distortion after vendor 3D corrections measured less than 1 mm within 10 cm and less than 2 mm within 20 cm of isocenter. Monthly phantom testing over 12 months confirmed geometric stability within established tolerances. A brain imaging protocol achieved 1 mm slice thickness on 3D T1-weighted acquisitions consistent with ISRS guidelines, with total scan time under 35 minutes. To date, 211 intracranial SRS patients have been scanned and treated to a total of 511 lesions with a median volume of 0.58cc [0.004 - 304.48 cc].…

items.title: Intensity-controlled Raster Scanning Carbon Ion Radiation Therapy With a Heavy-ion Gantry: Clinical Experience at Heidelberg Ion Beam Therapy Center
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Dvornikovich K, Held T, Franke H, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Carbon ions have biophysical advantages over photons, including a finite range, increased relative biological effectiveness, and lowered oxygen dependence. Maximum treatment flexibility is attainable with rotational beam delivery. We report our clinical experience using the carbon-ion gantry at the Heidelberg Ion Beam Therapy Center with intensity-controlled raster scanning capability, focusing on treatment toxicity. Methods And Materials: A total of 1622 patients treated using the carbon-ion gantry between 2012 and 2026 were evaluated. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Toxicity analysis was conducted using Common Terminology Criteria of Adverse Events v5.0. Results: The median age preradiation therapy was 59 years (range, 18-91). Most patients had locally advanced tumors (21.8% T4; 11.2% T3) without regional lymph node metastases (45.4% N0). The most common treatment indications were sacrococcygeal tumors (n = 331; 20.4%), followed by tumors of the paranasal sinuses (n = 166; 10.2%) and the spine (n = 121; 7.5%). A total of 486 patients (30.0%) received carbon-ion reirradiation, the most frequent carbon-ion gantry treatment indication viewed across all patients. The most common particle therapy beam-angle number was 2 (range, 1-7). The use of more than 2 beam angles was particularly frequent in tumors of the skull base (45.8%) and the thoracic region (40.0%). High-grade (III and IV) acute and late toxicity rates were 2.4% and 4.2% in primary treatment. Mean numbers of acute and late grade I and II toxicity events per patient were 2.2 (95% confidence interval, 2.0-2.4) and 2.0 (95% confidence interval, 1.7-2.4), respectively. Conclusions: Carbon-ion radiation therapy using a heavy-ion gantry resulted in favorable toxicity rates in specific indications. Further interdisciplinary research demonstrating the clinical benefit of carbon-ion radiation therapy is required. This study provides more evidence supporting particle therapy facilities and may serve as a foundation for prospective clinical trials.

items.title: Fuzuloparib plus apatinib maintenance in patients with platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer previously treated with first-line poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitor maintenance (FLASH): an exploratory phase II trial
items.authors: Lv M, Lu J, Ma X, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: Fuzuloparib, a poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitor, has demonstrated survival benefits as maintenance therapy in poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitor-naïve patients with platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer. This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of fuzuloparib combined with apatinib in patients with platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer who were previously treated with first-line poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitor maintenance. Methods: This single-arm, exploratory phase II trial enrolled adults with ovarian cancer who had received first-line poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitor maintenance and had responded to recent platinum-based chemotherapy. Participants received oral fuzuloparib (100 mg twice daily) plus apatinib (250 mg once daily) until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival. Results: Between April 2022 and January 2024, 28 patients (median age: 54.5 years) were enrolled. The median time since the most recent poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitor treatment was 5.4 months (interquartile range; 4.4-6.7). Bevacizumab was used in the most recent chemotherapy regimen in 60.7% of patients, and 85.7% achieved a partial response to the recent chemotherapy. With a median follow-up of 9.9 months, the median progression-free survival was 4.86 months (95% confidence interval 3.38 to 9.40). The median progression-free survival was 5.29 months (95% confidence interval 1.05 to 9.40) in patients who received bevacizumab and 4.53 months (95% confidence interval 2.4 to not reached) in those who did not. The median overall survival was 15.87 months (95% confidence interval 15.54 to not reached), although this estimate remained immature because of the limited number of observed events. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 32.1% of patients, most commonly decreased platelet count (14.3%) and anemia (10.7%). No cases of myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukemia, or treatment-related deaths were observed. Conclusions: This study is the first, to our knowledge, to evaluate dual oral therapy with fuzuloparib and apatinib in patients with platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer who were previously treated with first-line poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitor maintenance. Preliminary findings suggest anti-tumor activity with manageable toxicity, warranting further investigation. Trial Registration: chictr.org.cn: ChiCTR2200059352.

items.title: Molecular Residual Disease After Definitive Chemoradiotherapy in Locally Advanced Head and Neck Cancer: Clinical Value and Optimal Timing for ctDNA Assessment
items.authors: Bruixola G, Martín-Arana J, Gimeno-Valiente F, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Accurate post-treatment assessment after definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT) in locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA-HNSCC) remains challenging due to limitations of standard imaging. We evaluated the diagnostic performance, prognostic value and optimal timing of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for molecular residual disease (MRD) detection. Methods: Seventy-four patients with LA-HNSCC treated with definitive CRT were prospectively enrolled. Plasma samples were collected before treatment, at 8 and 12 weeks after CRT, and during follow-up. ctDNA was analysed using a plasma-only methylation-based assay. Diagnostic performance for recurrence detection and associations with progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were evaluated and compared with 12-week PET/CT findings. Results: Baseline ctDNA was detectable in 85.1% of patients. Among post-treatment timepoints, week-12 ctDNA showed the highest diagnostic accuracy for recurrence detection, with 69% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 100% positive predictive value, and 76% negative predictive value. Detectable week-12 ctDNA was associated with shorter PFS (HR, 6.44; 95% CI, 2.73-16.74; p<0.001) and OS (HR, 7.31; 95% CI, 2.80-22.31; p<0.001 ). Longitudinal ctDNA surveillance identified additional recurrences among patients with initially undetectable week-12 ctDNA. Exploratory analyses integrating PET/CT and ctDNA identified prognostically distinct PFS groups (log-rank P=0.033), with the greatest additional prognostic stratification observed among PET partial-responders. Conclusions: Plasma-only methylation-based ctDNA provided high-specificity prognostic information after definitive CRT in LA-HNSCC, particularly at week 12 and in PET partial-responders. ctDNA may complement PET/CT for post-treatment risk stratification, but should not be used as a stand-alone test to exclude recurrence.

items.title: Dose-Response Relationship of Stereotactic Radiosurgery for IDH-Wildtype Recurrent Glioblastoma: An International Multicenter Analysis
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Dono A, Alcantar O, Wei CZ, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Salvage stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for selected patients with recurrent IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (rGB) offers survival benefit, but optimal dosing remains undefined. We evaluated safety, efficacy, and dose-response relationships of single fraction SRS for rGB. Methods: We conducted a retrospective multicenter study of 271 consecutive patients with rGB treated with single-fraction SRS at first recurrence (2007-2025). Primary outcome was post-recurrence survival (PRS); secondary outcomes included overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Multivariable Cox regression, propensity score matching (PSM), and recursive partitioning analysis (RPA) were used to identify prognostic factors. Results: Median age was 61 years; 63% male. Median recurrent tumor volume was 3.0 cm³ (IQR, 0.8-8.7). Median single fraction SRS dose was 16 Gy (IQR, 14-19). Radiation necrosis and neurological deficits occurred in 5.5% and 8.2%, respectively. Median PRS, OS, and PFS were 12.3, 24.2, and 10.4-months. Higher SRS dose independently predicted longer PRS (HR 0.81/Gy; 95% CI 0.73-0.90, p<0.001). Dose escalation >19 Gy improved PRS (18.6 vs 11.3-months; p=0.002) without increased toxicity in PSM cohorts. MGMT methylation and unifocal recurrence were favorable prognostic factors. In the RPA, tumor volume was the primary prognostic factor; dose intensification benefited mainly patients with smaller tumors, while preserved performance status reduced risk in larger tumors. Kaplan-Meier curves confirmed clinically meaningful PRS stratification (p<0.001). Conclusions: SRS is safe and effective for select patients with first-recurrence GB. Higher prescription doses were associated with improved post-recurrence survival without added toxicity within the dose range and volumes studied with a substantial number of patients receiving bevacizumab within 30 days of SRS. Dose-intensified SRS may be considered in carefully selected patients with limited-volume recurrence and preserved performance status.

items.title: Radiotherapy Preparedness in Conflict Zones: The Lessons We Learned in Lebanon
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Eid T, Ayoub Z, Al-Bitar T, et al.
items.abstract: Radiotherapy is uniquely vulnerable during armed conflicts because it depends on immovable equipment, trained staff, daily patient travel, reliable infrastructure, and uninterrupted access to treatment records. We describe the experience of the Department of Radiation Oncology at the American University of Beirut during two episodes of intense conflict affecting Lebanon in 2024 and 2026. We specifically focus on the closure of a satellite clinic and how we managed the resumption of care for displaced patients. Based on this experience, we propose practical preparedness measures for radiotherapy services in conflict-prone regions, including live off-site patient registries, predefined transfer workflows, regional radiotherapy capacity mapping, triage concepts, financial agreements, national coordination, and a wartime escalation framework. Radiotherapy preparedness should be treated as a routine component of cancer care in unstable regions, not an emergency exercise begun only after treatment has already been interrupted.

items.title: Comparison of Early-Stage Breast Cancer Patients with Three or More Positive Sentinel Lymph Nodes Treated with Regional Nodal Irradiation Alone or with Completion Axillary Lymph Node Dissection with or without Regional Nodal Irradiation: A Population Based Study
items.authors: Lustig DB, Bayley C, Phan T, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The optimal management of patients with early-stage breast cancer who have ≥3 positive sentinel lymph nodes (SLNs) is unknown. Our study aims to determine whether there is a difference in recurrence free survival (RFS) and breast cancer specific survival (BCSS) in this patient population who were treated with regional nodal irradiation (RNI) alone versus completion axillary lymph node dissection (cALND)±RNI. Methods: A retrospective study using a prospectively collected provincial database was performed to identify patients with clinically node negative early-stage breast cancer who underwent breast surgery and had 3 or more positive SLNs between 2010 - 2017. Results: A total of 89 patients were included in our study. The median follow-up was 7.6 years (5.0-14.0). The overall recurrence rate was 28.1% (n=25/89) with axillary and distant recurrence rates of 3.4% (n=3/89) and 24.7% (n=22/89) respectively. Overall survival was 75.3% (n=67/89) and the BCSS was 77.5% (n=69/89). There was no difference in 5-year axillary recurrence (6.3% vs. 1.8%; p=0.26) or 5-year recurrence free survival (81.3% vs. 75.4%; p=0.53) between patients treated with RNI alone vs. cALND ± RNI. Furthermore, there was no difference in 5-year OS (87.5% vs. 82.5%; p=0.53) or 5-year BCSS (87.5% vs. 84.2%; p=0.67) between the two study cohorts. However, lymphedema was significantly less in the RNI alone group compared to cALND ± RNI cohort (3.1% vs. 21.1%; p=0.02). Conclusions: We found no differences in regional or distant recurrence rates nor survival in patients with early-stage breast cancer found to have ≥3 positive SLNs when treated with RNI alone versus cALND ± RNI. RNI alone was associated with significantly less lymphedema.

items.title: Alectinib as Neoadjuvant Treatment in Potentially Resectable Stage III Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase-Positive Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: ALNEO Phase II Trial (GOIRC-01-2020-ML42316)
items.authors: Leonetti A, Boni L, Gnetti L, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a heterogeneous disease with no single definitive therapeutic approach. The role of neoadjuvant tyrosine kinase inhibitors in stage III ALK-positive NSCLC remains unknown. The ALNEO study evaluated the activity and safety of perioperative alectinib in this population. Patients And Methods: ALNEO is an open-label, single-arm, multicenter phase II study enrolling treatment-naïve patients with potentially resectable stage III ALK-positive NSCLC. Patients received neoadjuvant alectinib 600 mg twice daily for 8 weeks, followed by surgery and adjuvant alectinib for up to 96 weeks. The primary end point was major pathologic response (MPR; ≤10% residual viable tumor cells) assessed by blinded independent central review. Secondary end points included pathologic complete response (pCR), objective response rate (ORR), event-free survival (EFS), disease-free survival (DFS), overall survival (OS), and safety. Results: From May 2021 to July 2024, 33 patients were enrolled. The median age was 62 years (range, 33-79), 70% were female, and 52% were never smokers. Clinical stage was IIIA in 64% and IIIB in 36%. All patients completed neoadjuvant treatment, and 28 (85%) underwent surgery, most commonly lobectomy (75%). R0 resection was achieved in 24 (86%). MPR was observed in 14 patients (42%; 95% CI, 26 to 61), including four pCRs (12%; 95% CI, 3 to 28). ORR was 67%. Adjuvant treatment was initiated in 26 (79%) patients. After a median follow-up of 26.8 months, median EFS, DFS, and OS were not reached; six patients (18%) experienced disease recurrence. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 9% and 27% of patients during neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment, respectively. Conclusion: The ALNEO study met its primary end point, suggesting perioperative alectinib as a feasible and active approach in potentially resectable stage III ALK-positive NSCLC.

items.title: Organ-preserving multimodal therapy for patients with high-risk upper tract urothelial carcinoma in China (DISTINCT-I): a single-arm, phase 2 trial
items.authors: Huang J, Hu H, Ng C, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Radical nephroureterectomy is the standard treatment for patients with high-risk upper tract urothelial carcinoma, but causes irreversible nephron loss and can limit subsequent systemic therapy. We aimed to assess a response-adapted kidney-preserving strategy integrating induction disitamab vedotin plus tislelizumab, selective kidney-sparing surgery, and longitudinal circulating tumour DNA and urinary tumour DNA monitoring in patients with localised high-risk upper tract urothelial carcinoma. Methods: DISTINCT-I was a single-arm, phase 2 trial conducted at two tertiary referral centres in China. Adults aged 18 years or older with histologically confirmed, localised, high-risk upper tract urothelial carcinoma (cT1-T3, N0-N1, M0), and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-2 received 2·0 mg/kg intravenous disitamab vedotin plus intravenous 200 mg tislelizumab once every 3 weeks for two to four cycles, followed by response-adapted kidney-sparing surgery when feasible. The primary endpoint was the 1-year kidney-intact event-free survival rate, assessed in the intention-to-treat population. Kidney-intact event-free survival was defined as the time from enrolment to the earliest occurrence of high-risk upper tract urothelial carcinoma recurrence, death from any cause, or conversion to radical nephroureterectomy. Safety was assessed in all patients who received at least one dose of study treatment and according to Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events and Clavien-Dindo classification. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05912816), and is ongoing. Findings: Between Sept 6, 2023, and Nov 15, 2024, 36 patients were assessed for eligibility; ten did not meet the eligibility criteria and six declined to participate. Of the 20 patients enrolled, 17 (85%) were male and three (15%) were female; all patients were Chinese. At data cutoff (Dec 31, 2025), median follow-up was 17·0 months (IQR 14·0-23·0). The 1-year kidney-intact event-free survival rate was 70% (95% CI 46-88; 14 participants). Grade 3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in two (10%) patients (fatigue in one and increased γ-glutamyl transferase in another). No grade 4-5 treatment-related adverse events, serious treatment-related adverse events, or treatment-related deaths occurred. Interpretation: This structured, multimodal, response-adapted strategy was associated with kidney preservation in selected patients with high-risk upper tract urothelial carcinoma.…

items.title: Serplulimab combined with nab-paclitaxel and epirubicin in high-risk, early HR+/HER2- breast cancer (HELEN-B 018): a multicentre, single-arm, phase 2 trial
items.authors: Dai H, Lu Z, Sun X, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: This phase 2 trial aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of serplulimab combined with nab-paclitaxel and epirubicin in high-risk, early HR+/HER2- breast cancer NCT06394661 Patients and Methods: This multicenter, single-arm, phase 2 trial was conducted in China at 6 hospitals. Patients were eligible if they were 18 years or older, with early HR+/HER2- breast cancer (T1c N1-3 or T2-4 any N), and Ki-67 ≥20%. Participants received intravenous nab-paclitaxel (260 mg/m2) plus intravenous epirubicin (75 mg/m2) on day 1, and intravenous serplulimab (4.5 mg/kg) on day 3 of the treatment cycle, every 3 weeks for 6 cycles. The primary outcome was the rate of pCR (defined as ypT0/is ypN0), assessed in the full analysis set. Results: 101 participants started trial treatment and were included in the full analysis set. pCR was achieved in 23 patients (22.8%, 95% CI 15.3%-32.4%). RCB 0 or 1 was achieved in 34 patients (33.7%, 95% CI 24.8%-43.8%). The pCR rate was higher in PD-L1-positive (combined positive score (CPS)≥1) tumors (44.4%, 95% CI 30.0%-59.9%) than in PD-L1-negative tumors (5.4%, 95% CI 1.4%-15.8%, P <0.001). During the neoadjuvant phase, 30 (29.7%) patients experienced grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events. No new safety signals were identified and there were no treatment-related deaths. Conclusions: Serplulimab combined with nab-paclitaxel and epirubicin showed anti-tumor activity and manageable safety in patients with HR+/HER2- breast cancer, and the pCR rate was higher in PD-L1-positive tumors. These findings support further evaluation of this regimen in randomized controlled trials.

items.title: Assessment of simulated respiratory gating based on external-to-internal motion prediction using a hybrid, adaptive deep-learning network
items.authors: Milewski A, Nie X, Li G
items.abstract: Purpose: To assess the accuracy, safety, and efficiency of respiratory-gated radiotherapy (RGRT) based on internal respiratory waveforms predicted by a hybrid long short-term memory (LSTM) deep-learning network, which adapts to breathing irregularities through the application of time-domain cross-correlation (TCC) to check and correct any residual phase/time shift in the LSTM predictions. Methods: The adaptive LSTM-TCC model was built in two steps: (1) subject-specific LSTM models were trained to predict internal diaphragm motion from external bellows motion using each of 10 subjects' concurrent waveforms (≥20 Hz, 3-10 min) acquired from four-dimensional magnetic resonance imaging (4DMRI) protocol scans and (2) near real-time TCC was applied to the LSTM predictions to check and correct any residual phase/time shifts to safeguard against new breathing irregularities beyond the training data in the mid-term (3-10 min) and long-term (20-30 min) datasets. The testing datasets comprised both the mid-term and long-term concurrent motion waveforms, and the external-to-internal motion predictions and gating quality assessments for each subject were evaluated and validated with the actual internal motion as the ground truth. The hybrid LSTM-TCC models were compared with LSTM, TCC, and native external-to-internal correlation models. The temporal gating accuracy (beam-off and beam-on) and beam-gating quality (missing-target rate: %harm, and beam-on efficiency: %effic) of the hybrid LSTM-TCC model were evaluated and compared with LSTM, TCC, and native predictions. Results: The hybrid LSTM-TCC models produced the highest long-term sustained correlations (C > 0.8, within 30 min), yielding the lowest %harm = 5 ± 6% and the highest %effic = 67 ± 15%, compared with the LSTM (%harm = 8 ± 8%, %effic = 65 ± 16%), the TCC (%harm = 29 ± 31%, %effic = 43 ± 19%), and the native (%harm = 37 ± 23%, %effic = 38 ± 14%). The hybrid LSTM-TCC models produced a high, sustained performance (C = 0.9 ± 0.1) without remodeling, regardless of new breathing irregularities, and the average temporal error of the predicted gating windows was ∆t < 0.3 s. Conclusion: This study assesses the simulated respiratory-gating qualities of four methods, demonstrating that the hybrid LSTM-TCC approach outperforms the native waveforms, the TCC method, and the LSTM models, yielding the highest correlation, gating accuracy, and %effic, but the least %harm.…

items.title: Efficacy of non-invasive mechanical ventilation to reduce organ motion for abdominal radiotherapy
items.authors: Visser J, Veldman JK, Parkes MJ, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Respiratory motion is a challenge in abdominal radiotherapy. Motion mitigation strategies include gating or tracking, abdominal compression and breath-holding. With non-invasive mechanical ventilation (NIMV) regular breathing patterns can be imposed at typically 30 or 60 breaths per minute (brpm). NIMV at these high frequencies and with smaller tidal volumes reduce respiratory motion. Adding positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to this regularized breathing also adds the advantage of increasing lung volume. The aim of this study was to compare respiratory motion of abdominal organs between free breathing and regularized breathing in volunteers. Methods: In two sessions on different days ten healthy volunteers were imaged during free breathing (FB), NIMV-imposed regularized breathing at a frequency of 30 (NIMV30) and 60 brpm with PEEP (NIMV60P). Alternating single-slice coronal and sagittal MR images were acquired with a frequency of 2.7 Hz during a period of 350 s. On a single image at mid-ventilation the liver, spleen and kidneys were delineated, if visible. Other images were deformably registered to this reference image, resulting in a deformation vector field for each image. Vector fields were used to determine the motion in each voxel of the reference image after excluding 5% outliers. For voxels in each organ a histogram of the motion was calculated. The motion of the voxels at the 10th percentile, median and 90th percentile was used to represent the motion of the organ. Organ motion was compared between FB and NIMV. Results: Sixty MRI scans were available for this study. For all organs, the caudal-cranial (CC) motion was significantly smaller during NIMV30 and NIMV60P compared to FB. The group median CC motion of the liver was 29 mm, 16 mm and 9 mm for FB, NIMV30 and NIMV60P, respectively; for the spleen 31 mm, 20 mm, 12 mm; for the right kidney 22 mm, 14 mm and 9 mm; for the left kidney 19 mm, 14 mm and 10 mm. Conclusions: Regularized breathing imposed by NIMV reduces organ motion considerably and, is therefore, an effective respiratory motion mitigation strategy for abdominal organ radiotherapy. Trial Registration: The study is registered in the ICTRP; NL-OMON24117. The registration date was March 29, 2021.

items.title: RapidArc dynamic versus IMRT and VMAT for endometrial cancer SIB radiotherapy
items.authors: Zhao Y, Zhang X, Wang X, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Radiotherapy with simultaneous integrated boost (SIB) for endometrial cancer requires highly conformal dose distributions to reduce toxicity. RapidArc Dynamic (RAD), a novel technique combining dynamic arc delivery with strategic gantry pauses, may improve organ-at-risk (OAR) sparing. Purpose: This study aimed to compare RAD with conventional IMRT and VMAT for endometrial SIB radiotherapy, specifically evaluating the OAR sparing capabilities of the RAD technique in endometrial cancer treatment. Materials And Methods: Thirty patients with high-intermediate risk endometrial cancer were retrospectively enrolled. Three plans (RAD, IMRT, VMAT) were generated per patient, prescribing 50.4 Gy to the planning target volume (PTV) and 61.6 Gy to the nodal clinical target volume (CTVn) in 28 fractions. Plans were evaluated for OAR dose constraints, conformity index (CI), 50% dose spillage ratio ([Formula: see text]), monitor units (MU), and modulation complexity score (MCS). Results: RAD plans demonstrated superior OAR sparing, with fewer and less severe constraint violations for the bladder, rectum, small intestine, and bone marrow compared to IMRT and VMAT (Mann-Whitney U test, P < 0.05). RAD achieved a significantly higher average CI (0.833) than two-arc VMAT (0.813) and demonstrated the lowest average [Formula: see text] (3.45) compared to both IMRT (3.86) and VMAT (3.67). Furthermore, while VMAT required the fewest MU (527.8), RAD (1314.7) used significantly fewer MU than IMRT (3334.0) and exhibited higher MCS, indicating less complex delivery than IMRT. Conclusions: RAD provides superior OAR protection and steeper dose fall-offs compared to VMAT, while maintaining high target dose conformity and potentially improving delivery efficiency. It represents a promising technique for endometrial SIB radiotherapy, combining the advantages of IMRT and VMAT. Clinical Trial Number: Not applicable.

items.title: Radiation Necrosis After Stereotactic Radiosurgery in Brain Metastases and Arteriovenous Malformations: A Comparative Systematic Review of Clinical Patterns, Risk Factors, and Biological Hypotheses
items.authors: Ruggeri L, Mandelli J, Lipani R, et al.
items.abstract: Aims: Radiation-induced injury is a major dose-limiting complication of stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS). However, clinical and temporal patterns may differ between neoplastic substrates, such as brain metastases (BMs), and vascular substrates, such as arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), although whether these differences reflect biology, treatment characteristics, or methodological factors remains uncertain. The aim of this study was to characterise and compare reported patterns of radiation-induced injury after SRS in BM and AVM cohorts. Materials And Methods: This Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-compliant systematic review synthesised 16 independent primary series published through 2025, comprising 8385 patients. Formal meta-analysis was not performed because of substantial heterogeneity in endpoint definitions, follow-up, and units of analysis. Radiation necrosis (RN), adverse radiation effects (AREs), and other radiation-related complications were extracted according to original study definitions and descriptively synthesised. Results: After exclusion of overlapping cohorts, reported event proportions ranged from 6.8% to 30.4% in BM cohorts and from 3.4% to 38.4% in AVM cohorts. These values represent descriptive summaries of study-level event frequencies and were not considered directly comparable because of heterogeneity in endpoint definitions, follow-up duration, unit of analysis, and competing mortality in BM cohorts. BM series generally reported events within the first 1-2 years after SRS/SRT, whereas the AVM series also documented very late complications, occurring up to 24 years after SRS. Deep white matter involvement remains a potential anatomical modifier requiring further validation, and no validated dose constraint can currently be recommended. Conclusions: Radiation-induced injury after SRS encompasses heterogeneous clinical and radiological manifestations whose reported frequency and timing differ between BM and AVM cohorts. Differences may reflect treatment geometry, dose-volume characteristics, substrate-specific clinical factors, follow-up duration, and endpoint definitions rather than intrinsic differences in radiosensitivity. Late radiation-related complications in AVM cohorts highlight the importance of prolonged clinical and imaging follow-up, whereas evidence does not support a prescriptive pathology-specific surveillance schedule.

items.title: Nonlinear association between cumulative mean dose to the taste-bud-bearing tongue mucosa and patient-reported taste dysfunction during head and neck IMRT
items.journal: Tech Innov Patient Support Radiat Oncol
items.authors: Shinozawa S, Saito T, Tomita T, et al.
items.abstract: Introduction: The during-treatment relationship between cumulative mean taste bud dose and taste dysfunction remains incompletely characterized. This retrospective pilot study examined site-related dose variation and nonlinearity of this relationship during head and neck intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT). Methods: Thirty-two patients with oropharyngeal (n = 13) or hypopharyngeal/laryngeal (n = 19) cancer received definitive IMRT (70 Gy in 35 fractions). Routine treatment diaries assessed three taste qualities at 10-Gy prescribed-dose milestones (total score, 0-6). Cumulative mean taste bud dose was calculated at each assessment using planning computed tomography contours of the tongue mucosa. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age and concurrent chemotherapy compared linear, quadratic, and piecewise forms. An exploratory analysis compared taste bud and extended oral cavity doses. Results: Despite a uniform prescribed-dose schedule, final mean taste bud dose differed by primary site (median, 42.2 Gy for oropharyngeal vs. 21.2 Gy for hypopharyngeal/laryngeal cancer). The 20-Gy piecewise model improved fit compared with quadratic and linear models. The score increased steeply below 20 Gy (1.99 points per 10 Gy; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.58-2.41) and less steeply above 20 Gy (0.95 points per 10 Gy, 95% CI, 0.42-1.48; both p < 0.001), with a significant change in slope (p < 0.001). Models using oral cavity dose showed similar fit and prediction errors, without a clear advantage for taste bud dose. Conclusion: Cumulative mean taste bud dose showed a nonlinear association with patient-reported taste dysfunction during treatment. These findings support prospective validation of taste-focused dose assessment and planning strategies, without interpreting 20 Gy as a definitive threshold.

items.title: New diagnostic criteria can inflate myelodysplastic syndrome survival estimates
items.authors: Giguère P, Fergusson D, Allan D, et al.
items.abstract: Survival in oncology is reported to be improving, often attributed to better detection, diagnostics and treatments. However, the impact of disease reclassification is largely ignored despite the potential for bias in historical comparisons. We used the Molecular International Prognostic Scoring System cohort to estimate the effect of introducing a Myelodysplastic Syndrome/ Acute Myeloid Leukemia (MDS/AML) category to the classification of Myelodysplastic Syndrome. Survival was compared between: (1) "MDS-2016" including all patients with ≤ 19% blasts and (2) "MDS-2022" restricted to patients with < 10% blasts, the latter simulating a cohort without MDS/AML. Median survival increased from 3.4 years (95%CI 3.1-3.9) to 4.3 years (95%CI 4.0-4.6) and 5-year survival from 39.0% (95%CI 36.5-41.6%) to 43.6% (95%CI 40.8-46.6%) all favouring MDS-2022. Thus, reclassification alone can produce a clinically meaningful apparent improvement in survival. Consideration of this effect is essential for interest-holders. Replication in other datasets and for other diseases is warranted.

items.title: Uncovering the patient burden in radiotherapy: routine symptom and problem screening with patient-reported outcome measures
items.authors: Roch C, Mueller E, Türker SM, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Screening of supportive care needs using patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) is being introduced in Germany as a certification standard for cancer care. We describe the symptom and problem burden identified by routine Integrated Palliative Outcome Scale (IPOS) screening in cancer patients referred to radiotherapy with a curative or palliative treatment intent. Methods: We conducted a retrospective chart review at the Department of Radiation Oncology of a comprehensive cancer center, including patients who presented for pretreatment radiotherapy consultation in 2023. Patient-reported symptoms and problems documented in the IPOS were analyzed and compared between individuals treated with curative versus palliative intent. Results: Of the 1580 patients treated in 2023, evaluable IPOS data were available for 1251 (79.1%; 860 curative, 391 palliative). High or very high levels of burden were more frequent among patients treated with palliative than with curative intent across physical (59.3% vs. 30.1%) and emotional domains (59.6% vs. 42.6%), whereas social needs were similar (27.1% vs. 33.3%). The most common physical burdens were weakness, impaired mobility, and pain. High disease-/treatment-related anxiety was common among both patients and their families. One-third of patients treated with curative intent and one in five patients treated with palliative intent reported no urgent needs. Conclusion: Routine IPOS screening was practicable and identified a substantial range of reported burdens in patients treated with both curative and palliative intent. Further refinement of the screening content, timing, and frequency may improve its applicability, whilst prospective studies should examine the relationship between the results and further interventions as well as the benefits.

items.title: Health-related quality of life in patients with solid cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors: the ARON-MOUSEION-18 systematic review and meta-analysis
items.authors: Ciccimarra F, Vitale E, Maistrello L, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) contributes to the value of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), but assessment and reporting remain heterogeneous. Methods: This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261330878). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for RCTs of adults with solid tumors comparing ICI-based regimens with non-ICI controls and reporting global HRQoL with the EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL scale or EQ-5D-3L/5L visual analogue scale (VAS). Pooling required a visit-specific adjusted between-group estimate with a 95% confidence interval (CI) or standard error. Random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood, Hartung-Knapp adjustment) were used. Clinical relevance was assessed using instrument-specific MID benchmarks. Results: Eighty-two RCTs were included: 42 in the quantitative and 40 in the narrative synthesis, 40 reported EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL, 10 EQ-5D-3L VAS, and 14 EQ-5D-5L VAS. All pooled trials evaluated anti-PD-1-based regimens. The pooled LSMD for EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL was 1.78 points (95% CI 0.71-2.86; p = 0.002; I2 =71.9%). Neither EQ-5D VAS differ significantly. Most trial-level estimates were below the MID, and no trial showed clinically meaningful deterioration. Favorable estimates were concentrated in open-label active-control, advanced/metastatic and lung cancer trials. Conclusion: Anti-PD-1-based therapy results in no clinically important difference in global HRQoL compared with non-ICI controls: the small average advantage is below the MID and concentrated in open-label active-control trials. Interpretation is shaped by trial design, comparator, setting, assessment timing, and incomplete PRO reporting. Standardized PRO reporting is needed across cancer settings and ICI classes.

items.title: Magnetic resonance thermometry-based estimation of equivalent radiation dose and tumour control probability in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia: a proof-of-concept and uncertainty study
items.authors: Carrapiço-Seabra C, Mingo Barba S, Godart J, et al.
items.abstract: To estimate the equivalent radiation dose in 2 Gy fractions (EQD2Gy) and tumour control probability (TCP) from probe based and magnetic resonance (MR) temperature measurements. In addition, we evaluate how uncertainties in MR thermometry affect these metrics in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia for locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC).Approach: Temperature data were collected from three patients with LACC treated with radiotherapy and MR guided deep hyperthermia (MRgHT). Intraluminal vaginal probes provided temperature measurements at surrogate locations, while MR thermometry enabled voxel-wise temperature mapping within the target volume. These data were used to estimate EQD2Gy and TCP for combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia treatments. To assess the robustness of MR-based estimates, systematic and random temperature errors were introduced into MR thermometry data using Gaussian error models to simulate artefacts. The resulting impact on temperature distributions, EQD2Gy and TCP was evaluated using standard deviation analysis and dose volume histograms.Main results: Probe-based temperatures ranged from 39.1-39.7 °C, resulting in EQD2Gy and TCP enhancements of 2.4-4.3 Gy and 20-57 %, respectively. MR-based temperatures were higher (39.4-40.3 °C), yielding EQD2Gy (3.4-7.1 Gy) and TCP (22-68 %). Systematic temperature errors produced changes of up to 2 Gy in EQD2Gy and 5 % in TCP. In contrast, random errors - more representative of typical MR thermometry artefacts - led to minimal deviations, with changes of approximately 0.2 Gy in EQD2Gy. Within clinically relevant temperature ranges, overall uncertainties remained limited to 0.7 Gy for EQD2Gy and 1 % for TCP.Significance: MR thermometry enables voxel-based estimation of biological treatment enhancement in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia. Despite inherent temperature uncertainties, MR-based EQD2Gy and TCP estimates remain robust within clinical accuracy limits, supporting their use for treatment evaluation and future hyperthermia-informed treatment planning.

items.title: Hepatic Arterial Infusion Floxuridine with Systemic Therapy for Liver-dominant Metastatic Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma: Results of the PANCPUMP Phase II Pilot Study
items.authors: Smith SM, Aubrey JM, Preihs R, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Hepatic progression is common in metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). We evaluated hepatic arterial infusion (HAI) floxuridine (FUDR) added to systemic chemotherapy in selected patients with synchronous liver-dominant metastatic PDAC. Methods: PANCPUMP was a prospective, single-center, single-arm phase II pilot study of 14 patients with synchronous PDAC liver metastases and stable disease or response after at least 2 months of systemic chemotherapy. Patients underwent HAI pump placement and received up to six 28 day cycles of HAI FUDR with systemic therapy. The primary endpoint was 1 year hepatic progression-free survival, with a prespecified target of 40%. Results: Seven patients (50%) remained free of hepatic progression at 1 year, meeting the primary endpoint. Median time to hepatic progression was 15.7 months when deaths without hepatic progression were censored; median all-site progression-free interval and overall survival were 14.5 and 14.0 months, respectively. Five patients (35.7%) survived at least 24 months. Biochemical hepatotoxicity was frequent; two delayed grade 3 gastroduodenal artery (GDA)/catheter-associated vascular complications occurred. Among 10 patients with paired European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Core Quality-of-Life questionnaire assessments, the mean global health/quality-of-life score was 69.2 at baseline and 70.0 at first follow-up (p = 0.91). Conclusions: HAI FUDR plus systemic therapy met the prespecified hepatic-control endpoint in a highly selected cohort. These proof-of-concept findings support further study of regional hepatic therapy alongside contemporary systemic treatment.

items.title: Beyond CBCT: real-time motion management in spine and non-spine bone SBRT using stereoscopic X-rays and surface guidance
items.authors: Gutiérrez A, Dierinck K, Everaert T, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for spine and non-spine bone metastases requires high precision due to sharp dose gradients and proximity to organs-of-interest. This study evaluates an image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) workflow combining stereoscopic X-rays (XR) and surface guidance (SG) for setup, positioning, and intra-fraction monitoring. Methods: We retrospectively analysed 92 bone metastases across 71 consecutive patients treated with SBRT (≤5 fractions). Patient setup and verification was performed with iterative XR and CBCT. Intra-fraction motion was monitored using stereoscopic gantry-triggered XR and continuous SG. Equivalence between XR and CBCT was evaluated using paired two one-sided tests. XR-SG correlations, sensitivity, and specificity of the monitoring system were analysed across anatomical regions. Results: XR and CBCT showed equivalence for all spinal and pelvic targets. Iterative setup XR reduced mean 3D residuals from 1.8±2.1mm down to 0.3±0.2mm. During beam delivery, 95% of intra-fraction XR verifications for spine and pelvis locations remained within 1.5mm/1.5°. SG showed strong correlations with XR in the lateral (r = 0.872) and roll (r = 0.881) directions, but moderate to weak agreement in directions affected by respiratory motion. Conclusions: Stereoscopic X-rays are a fast and efficient method to achieve sub-millimetre positioning accuracy equivalent to CBCT for spine and pelvis bone SBRT, effectively reducing setup residuals and intra-fraction errors and enabling the use of small margins. Tailored IGRT strategies are recommended to manage location-specific challenges like respiratory motion. Surface guidance functions as a complementary real-time alert of patient motion in between IGRT procedures.

items.title: Magnetically enhanced peak-to-valley dose ratio for megavoltage photon minibeam radiotherapy
items.authors: Walpen A, Volken W, Zhu C, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Orthovoltage minibeam radiotherapy (MBRT) emerged as a promising strategy to reduce normal tissue toxicities while providing equivalent or superior tumor control compared to homogeneous target irradiation. These benefits arise from the sub‐millimetric beam sizes and the highly heterogeneous dose distributions, typical for this technique. For MBRT operating at megavoltage (MV) photon energies, the lateral scattering of secondary electrons into the low dose regions poses a major limitation, compromising the therapeutic benefits observed in orthovoltage MBRT. Meanwhile, in presence of an inline magnetic field (IMF), parallel to the central axis of the incoming radiation beam, laterally scattered secondary electrons are forced onto helical trajectories around the magnetic field, thus being radially confined. Purpose Investigate in‐silico the effects of homogeneous IMFs with constant field strengths up to 15 T on MV‐photon minibeams, with a view to confining secondary electrons radially and thus enhancing the peak‐to‐valley dose ratio (PVDR) compared to the case where no IMF is applied. Methods Monte Carlo simulations were performed using a simplified minibeam beam model. A digital water phantom (10 cm x 10 cm x 15 cm) was employed. The feasibility of four different minibeam geometries with respect to the PVDR enhancement at 14 cm depth in water with IMFs (0, 1.5 and 7 T) was investigated with mono‐energetic (4, 10 and 18 MeV) photon minibeams. Out of the four geometries, the one for which the application of IMFs resulted in the most pronounced PVDR enhancement at 14 cm depth, was selected for the subsequent investigations. Using this geometry, the effects of IMFs up to 15 T on the PVDRs as a function of depth in water, were investigated for mono‐energetic (2.5, 4, 6, 10, 15 and 18 MeV) photon minibeams and for a flattened (FF) Varian TrueBeam 6 MV photon energy spectrum. Finally, PVDR enhancement was investigated in a clinically motivated brain cancer case using the TrueBeam 6 MV FF photon energy spectrum with IMFs up to 15 T. Results Out of the four investigated geometries, the most pronounced PVDR enhancement at 14 cm depth in water was observed using the geometry with 1.0 mm beamlet width, 5.0 mm center‐to‐center spacing combined with 4 MeV beam energy and a 7 T IMF, increasing the PVDR from 2.6 ± 0.1 at 0 T to 16.0 ± 0.8 at 7 T. With this geometry, PVDRs enhancements occurred along the entire phantom for all investigated energies.…

items.title: A condensed matter inspired framework for the FLASH effect in radiotherapy
items.authors: Shvydka D, Karpov V, Gupta N
items.abstract: Abstract Background The FLASH radiation treatment utilizes ultra‐high dose rates (UHDR) with short exposure times, while exhibiting a unique feature of reduced damage to healthy tissues (sparing effect). FLASH physics remains unknown. Purpose To develop a quantitative bio‐physical model of FLASH radiation treatment. Methods We explore a two‐phase system of cancer inclusions embedded in a healthy host. The important morphological difference between the phases is that the cancer phase is structurally disordered, while the healthy host material is more organized. Correspondingly, the recombination times for radiation generated charge carriers are much shorter in the cancer phase than in the normal tissue host phase. Results In the host material, the nonequilibrium charge density under UHDR can be high enough to form electron‐hole liquid suppressing generation of active radicals; hence, sparing effect. A disordered tumor phase renders channels producing radicals capable of cells destruction. The FLASH thresholds for dose and dose rates are predicted. Conclusions The proposed two‐phase model provides quantitative description of FLASH radiation treatment.

items.title: A Multi-Agent MLLM Framework for Imaging-Grounded Treatment Recommendation in Acute Ischemic Stroke
items.authors: Yan B, Li Z, Fan Y, et al.
items.abstract: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) requires rapid integration of multimodal imaging, contraindication screening, and treatment selection within minutes, yet real-world decision-making is limited by fragmented workflows and uneven specialist availability. We developed an imaging-grounded multi-agent multimodal large language model (MLLM) framework that emulates a multidisciplinary stroke team for structured treatment recommendation. The framework decomposes the AIS workflow into coordinated agents for triage, time-window assessment, multimodal imaging interpretation, contraindication screening, and final treatment recommendation, with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) incorporating evidence-grounded knowledge. We retrospectively evaluated the framework in 1,658 consecutive suspected-AIS cases from two centers. Compared with a single-prompt baseline, treatment recommendation accuracy improved from 0.636 to 0.755 with multi-agent coordination and further to 0.785 after RAG augmentation, while Macro-F1 increased from 0.562 to 0.732 and 0.768, respectively. The framework showed improvements in reperfusion pathways, more effectively retaining candidates for intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy. Imaging agent yielded sensitivity/specificity of 0.490/0.999 for non-contrast CT intracranial hemorrhage detection, 0.883/0.851 for CT angiography large-vessel occlusion identification, and 0.939/0.739 for CT perfusion deficit assessment. These results suggest that structured imaging-grounded multi-agent coordination enhances reliability and clinical alignment of MLLM-based decision support in AIS, supporting potential deployment in time-critical stroke care settings with limited specialist availability.

items.title: Preventive effect of compression on breast cancer-related lymphedema after docetaxel chemotherapy: a randomized controlled trial
items.authors: Yeo SM, Lim JY, Kim JY, et al.
items.abstract: The preventive value of compression sleeves during docetaxel remains unclear, despite concerns about docetaxel-induced edema increasing breast cancer-related lymphedema (BCRL) risk. This randomized controlled trial evaluated whether prophylactic sleeve use reduces BCRL incidence and characterized docetaxel-induced edema trajectory and quality of life (QoL) impact. Eighty-three women were randomized to an intervention group (IG, n = 41) wearing 15-21 mmHg medical-grade sleeves during and 3 months after docetaxel chemotherapy, or to a usual-care group (UG, n = 42). The primary outcome was 2-year cumulative BCRL incidence, and secondary outcomes included the extracellular water-to-total body water (ECW/TBW) ratio and QoL (FACT-Taxane). Over 2 years, 14 participants (16.9%) developed BCRL with no significant between-group difference (HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.31-2.66; P = 0.869). Preventive sleeves significantly reduced the ECW/TBW ratio and arm volume (P = 0.010 and P = 0.008, respectively), but these reductions did not translate into a lower BCRL incidence. Notably, docetaxel-induced edema resolved spontaneously by 3 months post-chemotherapy in all participants, regardless of group. IG reported significantly worse QoL at 3 and 6 months (Δ = -8.47 and -9.81). The dissociation between edema reduction and lymphatic outcomes suggests that transient docetaxel-induced edema is unlikely to be a primary driver of chronic lymphedema, although a preventive benefit cannot be firmly excluded given the wide confidence interval. These findings do not support routine prophylactic sleeve use and highlight the need for targeted prevention in anatomically high-risk patients.

items.title: Pain severity and setup error in palliative radiotherapy for spinal metastases: A secondary analysis of a prospective cohort
items.journal: Tech Innov Patient Support Radiat Oncol
items.authors: Aoyama T, Koide Y, Kitagawa T, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Patients receiving palliative radiotherapy for spinal metastases often have severe pain, which may impair positional stability during treatment. We evaluated whether pain severity is associated with setup error, and estimated setup margins stratified by spinal level and immobilization method. Materials And Methods: This secondary analysis used data from a prospective cohort (UMIN000044984) of patients who underwent three-dimensional conformal spinal radiotherapy at our institution. Only sites with pre-treatment CBCT and a recorded baseline numerical rating scale (NRS) pain score were included (376 sites, 270 patients). The three-dimensional vector setup error was calculated as √(SI2 + LR2 + AP2), where SI, LR, and AP denote the superior-inferior, left-right, and anterior-posterior translational errors. Pain was categorized as mild (NRS 0-4), moderate (5-6), or severe (7-10). Associations with setup error were assessed by the Kruskal-Wallis test and Spearman correlation. Setup margins were estimated using both |mean| + 2SD and |mean| + 3SD criteria per direction, stratified by spinal level and immobilization method. Results: Median 3D vector setup error was 0.52 cm (IQR, 0.36-0.75). Setup error did not differ across pain groups (Kruskal-Wallis P = 0.134; Spearman r = 0.088, P = 0.089). Spinal level was the main associated factor: cervical treatments (thermoplastic mask) had lower median error than thoracolumbar/sacral (TLS) treatments without immobilization (0.41 vs. 0.54 cm, P = 0.004). Estimated margins were approximately 1.0 cm (cervical) and 1.5 cm (TLS). Conclusions: Baseline pain severity was not associated with setup error in palliative spinal radiotherapy. Spinal level, which determined the immobilization method, was the factor most strongly associated with setup error. The proposed margins may serve as practical planning references, in settings without pre-treatment image guidance based on skin-mark alignment.
