items.title: Widening MR-only radiotherapy to patients with hip implants through deep learning-based synthetic CT generation
items.authors: Zala NC, Lapaeva M, Günther M, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: MR-based synthetic CT (sCT) generation has enabled MR-only workflows and reached clinical application for specific sites. However, most studies have excluded patients with metal implants due to signal loss and metal-induced artifacts. In this study, we evaluate the feasibility of using deep learning (DL) methods to generate sCT images from T1 Dixon MR images in patients with hip implants, expanding the applicability of MR-only radiotherapy. Materials And Methods: A retrospective analysis included 20 patients with pelvic tumors and total hip replacements, divided into 16 training (hip-implant-only dataset) and 4 test cases. Additionally, 16 implant-free cases were added to the training set for a mixed-dataset experiment to evaluate the impact of additional data on sCT quality. A Pix2Pix generative adversarial network was trained on 2D axial MR-CT pairs, and both image similarity and dosimetric differences, including dose-volume histogram (DVH) deviations and gamma index, were assessed. Results: The generated sCT closely matched the CT, with DL models demonstrating promise in reconstructing both soft tissue and hip implants despite MR signal loss. For the best-performing investigated models, all mean DVH dose differences were below 0.5% with no outliers exceeding clinically acceptable limits of 2%, and mean 1%/1 mm gamma pass rates exceeded 98%. Although the mixed-dataset configuration exhibited lower standard deviations, no statistically significant differences were observed. Conclusions: These findings indicate that DL networks, specifically Pix2Pix, are capable of generating accurate pelvic sCTs for patients with hip implants, supporting further development of MR-only radiotherapy workflows for previously challenging anatomies.

items.title: Treatment-position magnetic resonance imaging reduces bony-landmark co-registration error in head and neck radiotherapy
items.authors: Itonaga T, Mikami R, Okubo M, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Routine diagnostic magnetic resonance imaging is acquired without immobilisation, creating co-registration uncertainty with planning computed tomography. We quantified whether treatment-position imaging reduced bony-landmark co-registration error, and whether the benefit persisted after resampling and deformable refinement. Materials And Methods: Fifty patients with paired treatment-position and diagnostic magnetic resonance imaging were retrospectively analysed. Each magnetic resonance imaging dataset was separately registered to planning computed tomography. Mean Euclidean distance between corresponding bony landmarks on the computed tomography and magnetic resonance images was compared after rigid registration and after deformable refinement, using Holm-adjusted landmark-wise comparisons. Through-plane resampling was assessed in all 50 patients, and interobserver reproducibility in a 15-patient subset. Results: Treatment-position imaging reduced mean Euclidean distance from 7.5 to 4.1 mm after rigid registration (difference 3.4 mm; 95% confidence interval 2.7-4.1; p = 2.0 × 10-13). The benefit persisted after resampling (4.3 mm) and deformable refinement (3.4 versus 6.0 mm; difference 2.6 mm; 95% confidence interval 2.1-3.1; p = 7.1 × 10-14), although refinement reduced the advantage by 0.8 mm (interaction p = 0.023). Intraclass correlation coefficients were 0.81 for diagnostic imaging and 0.48 for treatment-position imaging (95% confidence interval - 0.05-0.79), with small mean bias and lower treatment-position error in all 15 patients. Conclusions: Treatment-position magnetic resonance imaging reduced bony-landmark error in co-registration with planning computed tomography after rigid registration, and the benefit persisted after deformable refinement. Because delineation and dose-volume parameters were not assessed, these findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating improved contouring accuracy.

items.title: An EPID-based virtual audit framework for multi-institutional radiotherapy audits using direct fluence comparison
items.authors: Kishigami M, Adachi T, Ishihara Y, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: The complexity of volumetric modulated arc therapy highlights the need for robust quality assurance in multi-institutional clinical trials. Although electronic portal imaging device-based virtual audits are scalable, standardized workflows and evaluation criteria remain lacking. This study developed and evaluated a virtual audit framework comparing radiotherapy plan-derived and electronic portal imaging device-derived fluence maps. Material And Methods: Forty-one volumetric modulated arc therapy datasets from 15 institutions were analyzed. Plan-derived fluence maps were generated by convolving opening density matrices with a double-Gaussian electronic portal imaging device response kernel, while integrated portal images served as detector-derived fluence maps. Vendor-specific common parameters were evaluated using leave-one-machine-out validation, excluding each held-out machine's parameters before recalculating vendor-level parameters. Multileaf collimator positional, collimator-angle, and monitor-unit errors were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results: Mean gamma passing-rate differences ranged from -0.015 to 0.018 percentage points for Varian systems and from 0.387 to 1.018 percentage points for Elekta systems. The 3%/1 mm criterion yielded areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves of 0.959, 0.938, and 0.898 for multileaf collimator positional, collimator-angle, and monitor-unit errors, respectively, and produced the highest values for multileaf collimator positional and collimator-angle errors. A 95% gamma passing rate threshold at 3%/1 mm provided high sensitivity, whereas 90% at 3%/2 mm provided high specificity. Conclusions: Leave-one-machine-out validation supported the feasibility of vendor-level parameter standardization, potentially reducing machine-specific optimization. A preliminary tiered framework combining 95% at 3%/1 mm and 90% at 3%/2 mm may identify cases requiring review in multi-institutional radiotherapy audits.

items.title: "They'll do the right thing": Patient perceptions of safety and patient-centered care in radiation oncology - a qualitative interview study
items.journal: Tech Innov Patient Support Radiat Oncol
items.authors: Baehr A, Christalle E, Schwenzer F, et al.
items.abstract: Introduction: Although data highlight the high relevance of perceived safety, comprehensive insights into this concept from the patient's perspective remain scarce, particularly in radiation oncology. During the development of patient safety indicators, participants emphasized multiple facets of perceived safety that closely intersected with core principles of patient-centered care. Consequently, this secondary qualitative analysis aimed to examine patients' conceptualization of patient safety in radiation oncology and investigate the underlying dimensions of patient-centered care that shape their sense of safety. Methods: A secondary qualitative analysis was performed on semi-structured interviews with nine patients recruited at an academic radiation oncology center. The study was originally conducted to define patient safety indicators in radiation oncology. The primary focus was placed on evaluating patients' overall perceptions of safety within the radiotherapy setting, as well as identifying recurring themes that patients identify as important for patient safety but are related to patient-centered care. Results: Patients described three key aspects in their definition of safety: to be treated correctly (right dose in the right place), to perceive healthcare professionals as experts, and to work with professionals in a spirit of trust. Six major dimensions of patient centeredness were predominantly mentioned: "Patient information", "coordination and continuity of care", "patient safety", "essential characteristics of the clinicians", "clinician-patient communication" and "clinician-patient relationship". Patients were furthermore able to describe situations when they felt insecure as well as suggestions for improvements. Conclusion: This study was able to define the construct of patient safety in radiation oncology from the patients' perspective. It also underlined the major dimensions of patient-centered care aspects which might lead to perceived safety. The radiation therapy community should focus future efforts on actively involving patients in patient safety and strengthening safe care through patient-centered care. Limitations: Since this study was a secondary analysis with a limited sample size, the findings should be validated in a larger multicenter prospective study specifically designed for this purpose.

items.title: Assessment of systemic redox status in breast cancer patients receiving radiotherapy: a thiol/disulfide and nitrosative stress perspective
items.authors: Kavak AG, Karslioglu I, Demiryürek S, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Breast cancer (BC) is associated with chronic oxidative and nitrosative stress, yet the systemic effects of adjuvant radiotherapy on redox balance remain insufficiently defined. This prospective observational study evaluated serum thiol-disulfide homeostasis and nitrosative stress markers in women receiving adjuvant radiotherapy for breast cancer, with the aim of determining whether treatment was associated with a short-term systemic biomarker change. Methods: Thirty-nine women with stage II BC received adjuvant conformal radiotherapy to 50 Gy in 25 fractions, and 39 age-matched healthy women served as controls. Venous blood samples were obtained immediately before radiotherapy and 24 h after the last fraction to evaluate native thiol, total thiol, disulfide, nitric oxide (NO), and 3‑nitrotyrosine (3-NT) levels. Results: At baseline, native and total thiol concentrations were significantly lower in patients than in healthy controls (p < 0.001 and p < 0.01, respectively), whereas disulfide levels were higher (p < 0.05). Nitric oxide and 3‑nitrotyrosine levels were also significantly higher in patients (both p < 0.001). None of the measured biomarkers changed significantly from pre-RT to post-RT (all paired p > 0.05), and post-treatment values remained significantly different from control levels. Conclusion: Breast cancer patients showed differences in systemic thiol-disulfide and nitrosative stress markers compared with healthy controls, and these differences remained present 24 h after the final radiotherapy fraction. However, no statistically detectable within-patient change was observed over the sampled interval. The clinical relevance of these biochemical findings should be evaluated in longitudinal studies incorporating standardized toxicity assessment, patient-level dosimetry, and oncologic outcome data.

items.title: Combination of BVAC-C and durvalumab in recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer: a phase II study
items.authors: Choi CH, Lee JW, Kim TJ, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors show limited efficacy in previously treated recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer (rmCC). BVAC-C is an autologous B cell-based and monocyte-based therapeutic vaccine targeting human papillomavirus (HPV)16/18 E6 and E7 oncoproteins. Methods: We report a phase II trial—representing the first clinical evaluation of a B cell– and monocyte-based therapeutic HPV vaccine combined with a programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor—evaluating BVAC-C combined with durvalumab in patients with HPV16/18-positive rmCC who had progressed after platinum-based chemotherapy. This single-arm, open-label, two-part phase II trial was registered prospectively at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04800978) on 15 March 2021, before enrollment of the first participant. Results: 30 patients received treatment; 29 were evaluable for efficacy. The objective response rate (ORR) was 37.9% (six complete responses and five partial responses), and the disease control rate was 62.1%. The 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate was 51.7% and median PFS was 8.7 months (95% CI 4.0 to 24.3 months). Patients with a treatment-free interval >6 months achieved a significantly higher ORR (52.9% vs 16.7%; p=0.047). Notably, the median duration of response was 20 months and complete responders showed sustained remission beyond 18 months, raising the possibility of functional cure in a subset of patients. Antigen-specific T-cell responses and cytokine activation were robust and PD-L1-independent. Conclusions: BVAC-C plus durvalumab showed encouraging antitumor activity with a manageable safety profile, supporting further evaluation in HPV-positive rmCC. Trial Registration Number: NCT04800978.

items.title: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab in surgically resectable hepatocellular carcinoma (PRIME-HCC): a prospective, phase 1b, single-arm trial and translational analyses
items.authors: D'Alessio A, Fulgenzi CAM, Pai M, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab improves survival in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. We evaluated this combination as neoadjuvant therapy and investigated its effect on peripheral immunity and the tumour microenvironment. Methods: PRIME-HCC is a single-arm, phase 1b trial in adults (aged ≥18 years) with early-stage resectable hepatocellular carcinoma, Child-Pugh A liver function, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-1. Patients received nivolumab (3 mg/kg intravenously on days 1 and 22 of the first and second cycle) and ipilimumab (1 mg/kg intravenously on day 1 of the first cycle only) before liver resection. The primary endpoint was safety, assessed by treatment-related delays to surgery and adverse events in the intention-to-treat population. Translational analyses included imaging mass cytometry and spatial transcriptomics on paired tumour samples, peripheral immunophenotyping, T-cell receptor (TCR) β sequencing, and longitudinal tumour-agnostic circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) profiling. This trial was registered with EudraCT (2018-000987-27) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03682276); follow-up is currently ongoing. Findings: Between Sept 18, 2019, and Sept 28, 2023, of 43 patients assessed for eligibility, 33 patients were enrolled (25 [76%] male and 8 [24%] female; median age 68 years [range 38-80; IQR 63-73]); median follow-up was 25·7 months (95% CI 21·2-30·1). Any-grade adverse events occurred in 31 (94%) of patients, with treatment-related adverse events (trAEs) in 25 (76%) patients. Grade 3 trAEs occurred in three (9%) patients (transaminase elevation, anaemia, and dyspnoea). Serious adverse events were recorded in three (9%) patients, and no grade 4-5 events or treatment-related deaths occurred. 30 (91%) patients underwent surgery, including two (6%) who had immune checkpoint inhibitor-related surgical delays. Objective response rate by RECIST 1.1 was noted in eight (25%; 95% CI 13-42) patients (one complete response and seven partial responses), with 31 (97%; 84-100) patients achieving disease control. items.title: Multimodal multitask deep learning for predicting tertiary lymphoid structures and peritoneal recurrence in gastric cancer: a multicentre development, validation, and testing study
items.authors: Li Z, Zhang T, Wang W, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Peritoneal recurrence remains a common and fatal complication following curative gastric cancer surgery. Tertiary lymphoid structures are crucial indicators of immune response in cancer, and their maturation is associated with better prognosis and therapy outcomes. Evaluation of these structures could improve patient stratification for treatment of cancer but is hindered by the invasive and biased nature of histological methods. This study aimed to explore a non-invasive radiological method of assessment in patients with gastric cancer, using a novel multitask hybrid model to predict the presence and maturation status of tertiary lymphoid structures and peritoneal recurrence-free survival. Methods: We developed CTransNet, a multitask hybrid model combining a convolutional neural network (ResNet50) and a Transformer model to predict tertiary lymphoid structure maturation and peritoneal recurrence-free survival in patients with gastric cancer. The study used retrospective data from eight Chinese cohorts of patients treated for gastric cancer at Nanfang Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, Yunnan Cancer Hospital, and Guangdong Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine (one training cohort, two internal validation cohorts, three external validation cohorts, and two independent cohorts of patients treated with anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 inhibitors for at least two cycles). Patients were classified into three categories based on the presence and maturation of tertiary lymphoid structures (identified using haematoxylin-eosin and immunohistochemistry staining): TLS0 (absent tertiary lymphoid structures), TLS1 (primary follicle-like tertiary lymphoid structures without germinal centres), and TLS2 (secondary follicle-like tertiary lymphoid structures with germinal centres [ie, more mature structures]). Peritoneal recurrence was assessed using imaging (ultrasonography, CT, or PET-CT), clinical signs, or reoperation. We evaluated the accuracy of the multitask hybrid model in classifying patient-level tertiary lymphoid structure status using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Patients were stratified into risk groups using the median predicted score from the training cohort (high vs low), which was then applied to the validation cohorts. Survival outcomes (peritoneal recurrence-free survival, disease-free survival, and overall survival) were analysed using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox proportional hazards models. We also analysed the relationships between predicted scores and responses to chemotherapy and immunotherapy.…

items.title: Enhanced diffusion model with 3D structural and segmentation priors for lung cancer radiotherapy dose prediction
items.authors: Cobilean V, Mavikumbure H, Drake D, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: Diffusion models show strong potential for high-fidelity radiotherapy dose prediction, but their performance depends heavily on the conditioning mechanism. This study introduces a novel conditioning strategy that improves volumetric consistency in slice-wise dose generation while reducing reliance on manually annotated organ-at-risk (OAR) masks. Approach: We propose a diffusion-based dose prediction framework conditioned on features from the full 3D computed tomography (CT) volume and a pre-trained medical image segmentation model. A 3D feature extractor encodes global anatomical information from the entire CT volume to preserve spatial coherence across 2D dose predictions. Rather than relying on manual OAR masks, the model uses anatomical representations from the pre-trained segmentation network, integrated via cross-attention to enable anatomy-aware dose prediction. Main Results: The framework, Diff-Seg3D, was evaluated on three lung cancer radiotherapy datasets representing Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT), Fixed Gantry Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (FGIMRT), and 3D Conformal Radiation Therapy (3DCRT) planning techniques. It achieved the numerically lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on all three datasets, with values of 3.16, 4.38, and 4.02 Gy, respectively, and the best dose-volume histogram (DVH) scores (2.64 and 3.82) on VMAT and FGIMRT, while remaining competitive on 3DCRT. Pre-trained 3D anatomical and segmentation encoders improved the baseline diffusion model, with segmentation features improving performance without requiring explicit OAR contours at inference. Significance: This conditioning strategy improves volumetric consistency and anatomical awareness in diffusion-based dose prediction. The framework can serve as a tool for generating treatment-specific, anatomy-conditioned dose priors to guide radiotherapy planning.

items.abstract: Large-scale screening for leukemia remains challenging due to the absence of simple, scalable, and intelligent tools. Here, we present LeukoAlert, an artificial intelligence framework that transforms routine complete blood count (CBC) data (72 features) into a real-time opportunistic screening and risk flagging tool. Trained and validated on 446,558 records from 203,284 individuals across seven independent centers, the model achieved high discrimination between leukemia and non-leukemia cases (area under the curve (AUC) up to 0.996), with moderate performance for acute versus chronic subtype classification. items.abstract: ObjectiveOsteosarcoma is a rare primary bone cancer of adolescents and young adults without significant improvement in treatments or outcomes in several decades. Resection is standard of care for recurrent disease. Patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection (LOOR-FSR) may present the most meaningful opportunity for impactful intervention but alternative trial endpoints to objective response are needed. Here we update benchmarks for LOOR-FSR with contemporary clinical trial data. Patients/MethodsThis study included patients with pathologically confirmed LOOR-FSR enrolled on three Childrens Oncology Group phase 2 single arm trials. Benchmark endpoints assessed in this patient population were event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS). In addition, we evaluated the impact of demographics and baseline clinical factors on outcome. ResultsNinety-nine patients met criteria for inclusion in this analysis. Median EFS and OS were 4.8 (95% CI: 3.5, 6.3) and 26.2 (23.3, 56.8) months respectively. Twelve-month EFS was 22% (15-31%) and ranged from 14% to 29% across the 3 trials, a difference that did not achieve statistical significance. The risk of EFS event was higher for those whose first recurrence occurred within two years of diagnosis (p=0.009). Other demographic and clinical factors did not statistically impact risk of event though estimated EFS for males was lower than for females. ConclusionDespite almost doubling the number of patients in this historical control cohort, wide variance in outcomes led to confidence intervals unchanged from previously published work. Until the most significant factors contributing to variability of outcomes in this patient population are quantified, single arm trials of new approaches will only be able to identify large effect sizes. Smaller effect sizes will require randomization.

items.title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist use and overall survival in endometrial cancer: a multicenter propensity score-matched cohort study
items.authors: Yousif A, Elchouemi M, Asad AB
items.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the association between glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) use and overall survival in women with endometrial cancer. Methods: Using the TriNetX network, we identified women aged 18-75 years with endometrial cancer diagnosed between 2018 and 2024 and propensity score matched those with a GLP-1RA record within 12 months before diagnosis to women without prior use, with follow-up anchored to the date of diagnosis. A 2-year landmark analysis compared new GLP-1RA use within 2 years of diagnosis with no use among women alive at 2 years without evidence of advanced disease, and sensitivity analyses included an active comparator, race-stratified analyses and a negative-control outcome. The outcome was 5-year all-cause mortality. Results: In the primary analysis (2646 matched pairs), 5-year survival was 91.6% among GLP-1RA users and 90.2% among non-users (hazard ratio [HR] 0.81; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65-1.02), and in the 2-year landmark analysis (2275 pairs) it was 96.4% and 96.3% (HR 0.92; 95% CI, 0.63-1.34). Results were similar against dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (HR 0.91; 95% CI, 0.45-1.84) and by race (interaction P = 0.46), whereas a comparison with women who never received a GLP-1RA, as in previous studies, yielded an HR of 0.58 (95% CI, 0.48-0.70). Conclusions: Once follow-up was anchored to the date of diagnosis, GLP-1RA use was not associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality in women with endometrial cancer, and these hypothesis-generating findings should temper the extrapolation of survival associations reported in other cancers until prospective trials are completed.

items.title: Effect of radiotherapy on cardiac implantable electronic devices - evaluation of potential explanatory variables in more than a decade
items.authors: Christiansen A, Müller-Leisse J, Hillmann HAK, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: As the population ages, an increasing number of patients are undergoing radiotherapy with an implanted cardiac device. Therefore, ensuring the safety of these devices during radiotherapy is crucial. This study aims to analyse the effect of radiotherapy on such devices, with a particular focus on changes in lead variables. Methods: This retrospective study examined all patients with a cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) who underwent radiotherapy at a single institution between 2012 and 2022. Device function and associated changes in lead parameters were analysed before and after radiotherapy. Results: The study cohort included 279 patients who underwent 310 courses of radiotherapy. During the 11-year study period, one device failure requiring replacement due to a software error was recorded. This occurred following irradiation with 15 MV photons. Changes in individual lead parameters were more common, occurring in almost half of all radiotherapy courses. Lead impedances were particularly sensitive to changes, with high-voltage impedances being affected more frequently (61% of impedances) than other impedances. Sensing, pacing thresholds, and battery voltage were less frequently affected, with changes occurring in fewer than 10% of the analysed leads or batteries. None of the observed changes manifested as clinical symptoms. There was no statistically significant association between radiation parameters and the observed changes in lead values with only a few courses using neutron-generating photon energies. Furthermore, no dose-effect relationship for device doses could be established. Receiving multiple courses of radiotherapy in one year or over several years did not increase the risk to the device or cause greater variation in lead variables. Conclusion: Only one safety event occurred during the observation period, resulting in an error rate of 0.4% across 11 years and 279 patients. Changes in individual lead parameters were more frequent. However, no clear association could be established between the observed changes and radiation parameters. In particular, changes in lead variables were not explained by the dose to the device or repeated courses of radiotherapy. Therefore, the risk to the safety and function of cardiac devices from radiotherapy appears to be small.

items.abstract: Importance: Long-term lung cancer (LC) survivors remain at risk of LC events (LCEs), including late recurrence and second primary LC, beyond 5 years after diagnosis, but the role of computed tomography (CT) surveillance beyond 5 years remains uncertain. Objective: To evaluate whether CT receipt beyond 5 years after LC diagnosis is associated with LCEs and survival. Design, Setting, And Participants: This nationwide population-based cohort study used sequential target trial emulation with monthly eligibility reassessment and time-updated propensity score matching based on data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. Patients diagnosed with LC from 2006 to 2019 were followed up through December 31, 2024. Long-term LC survivors were eligible for trial entry 5.5 years after diagnosis if they had no administrative evidence of active or recurrent LC, a prior LCE, or another primary cancer. Data were analyzed between January 1, 2026, and February 28, 2026. Exposures: CT receipt beyond 5 years after LC diagnosis, defined as chest CT during the 1-month assessment window at each monthly trial baseline, compared with no CT receipt. Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome was LCE occurrence, defined by new LC-specific special copayment registration after the monthly trial baseline. Secondary outcomes were all-cause mortality, surgical resection after LCE detection, and subsequent mortality. Results: The cohort of 55 694 LC survivors (mean [SD] age, 63.3 [10.9] years; 58.0% male) contributed 2 629 462 eligible person-trials. Matching yielded 583 756 person-trials per group. During a median (IQR) follow-up of 2.74 (1.16-5.18) years, CT receipt was associated with a higher incidence of LCEs (2.49% vs 1.97% per year; hazard ratio [HR], 1.28 [95% CI, 1.26-1.29]) and lower all-cause mortality rate (2.62% vs 4.33% per year; HR, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.65-0.67]) compared with no CT receipt. Among patients with an LCE, CT receipt was associated with greater odds of surgical resection after LCE (odds ratio, 1.46 [95% CI, 1.41-1.52]) and a lower subsequent mortality risk (HR, 0.63 [95% CI, 0.61-0.64]). These associations were observed more frequently among females (HR, 0.47 [95% CI, 0.44-0.49]), older adults (HR, 0.57 [95% CI, 0.54-0.60]), and never smokers (HR, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.53-0.57]). items.title: The emerging role of dosimetry in theranostics
items.authors: The Cancer Letter Administrator
items.abstract: Theranostics is a rapidly growing field that is moving toward a more quantitative and individualized treatment strategy, particularly for therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals. Radiopharmaceuticals are compelling because they combine biology and radiation. Typically a small molecule or antibody binds to a molecular target on a cancer cell and carries various types of radiation directly to it, such as Lutathera for neuroendocrine cancers and Pluvicto for prostate cancer. One of the most important developments is the growing evidence that the radiation dose absorbed by a tumor predicts response and clinical outcomes. Through imaging-based dosimetry, we can measure uptake and estimate how much radiation reaches tumors and normal tissues, creating a path to personalize treatment rather than relying solely on standardized administration. Dosimetry as the next frontier Radiation oncologists have long understood that tumor control is tied to the delivered radiation dose. The same principle increasingly applies to radiopharmaceutical therapies. Pretreatment and post-treatment imaging may help determine whether a patient is likely to receive a meaningful tumor dose. For decades, pretreatment imaging has been used for patients with thyroid cancer who receive radioactive iodine, or RAI, to determine the initial treatment dose. More recently, post-treatment imaging has been used to map radiation doses in patients receiving transarterial radioembolization, or TARE, for liver cancer. If the field builds the evidence and infrastructure collaboratively, theranostics can more quickly become a precise and integrated part of cancer care and improve outcomes for our cancer patients. Post-treatment imaging potentially can show how much of the agent a tumor has absorbed and identify lesions that may be undertreated and require other ablative approaches, such as stereotactic body radiation therapy or needle ablation. This evolution mirrors external beam radiation therapy, where treatment planning and dose optimization are central to balancing efficacy and toxicity. Patients can absorb and distribute radiopharmaceuticals differently based on a number of factors, such as differences in circulation, perfusion, tumor penetration, clearance, metabolism, and tumor biology, including the expression of the molecular target. As a result, lesions within the same patient may have markedly different uptake and subsequent response. Dosimetry gives us an opportunity to adjust treatment to that biology.…

items.authors: Hsiao YY, Lu CC, Kao HC, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To compare filtered back projection (FBP), 50% Adaptive Statistical Iterative Reconstruction-Veo (ASiR), and medium-strength deep learning image reconstruction (DLIR) for hydroxyapatite calcification inserts under different dose, tube-voltage, and phantom-size conditions using contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), background noise magnitude, and noise power spectrum (NPS) analysis. Methods: A QRM-Thorax containing a QRM-CCI D100 cardiac calcification insert was scanned on a GE Revolution Apex CT system using institution-defined routine and low-dose protocols at 80, 100, 120, and 140 kVp, with and without an Extension Ring L. Images were reconstructed at 2.5-mm thickness using FBP, ASiR, and DLIR. CNR was evaluated for 3- and 5-mm inserts at 200, 400, and 800 mg HA/cm3. Background noise was assessed from a calcification-excluded mask. For NPS analysis, 10 calcification-free images were analyzed for each acquisition condition. Total two-dimensional NPS power, power-weighted normalized radial NPS, and power-weighted mean spatial frequency were calculated. Results: DLIR reduced background noise magnitude and increased CNR relative to FBP across the evaluated conditions, whereas differences relative to ASiR varied with insert size, density, tube voltage, and phantom size. Across all 16 protocol, phantom-size, and tube-voltage combinations, ASiR and DLIR reduced total 2D NPS power by 58.1% and 75.8%, respectively, relative to FBP; DLIR reduced total power by 41.9% relative to ASiR. ASiR produced a more consistent shift toward lower power-weighted mean spatial frequencies, averaging 12.4% below FBP, whereas the shift with DLIR was smaller and more condition dependent, averaging 3.2% below FBP. Conclusions: In this controlled phantom study, DLIR reduced total noise power and improved CNR relative to FBP, but its incremental difference from ASiR was task and protocol dependent.
